Common minor side effects include water retention and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. This favorable safety profile is noted in the trace as relevant to the potential evaluation of creatine as an adjunct in oncology settings, where tolerability is a central concern.

label: Skeletal Muscle
description: Approximately 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, where it exists partly as free creatine and partly as creatine phosphate. The muscle creatine pool is maintained by both endogenous synthesis and dietary intake, and it is depleted by high-intensity activity and resynthesized during recovery. Muscle total creatine concentrations can be increased by supplementation, typically by 10-20 percent, and this elevated store extends the time for which high-intensity exercise can be sustained. The predominance of skeletal muscle as a creatine depot explains why most creatine research has focused on muscle function, strength, and performance.

label: Amino Acids
description: Creatine is synthesized endogenously from the amino acids arginine, glycine, and methionine in a two-step pathway. The first step, catalyzed by arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), takes place primarily in the kidney and pancreas and produces guanidinoacetate; the second step, catalyzed by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate in the liver, producing creatine. This biosynthetic origin connects creatine metabolism to the methylation cycle and one-carbon metabolism, a connection relevant to hypotheses linking creatine status to epigenetic regulation and cancer risk.

label: Arginine
description: Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound synthesized endogenously in the body. The first step of its biosynthesis condenses arginine and glycine into guanidinoacetate (GAA), a reaction catalyzed by arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), which is expressed in the kidney, pancreas, liver, and certain brain regions. Endogenous synthesis supplies roughly half of the daily creatine requirement; the remainder must come from the diet, primarily red meat and fish, or from supplements. Deficiencies in the enzymes of this pathway (AGAT, GAMT) or the creatine transporter produce creatine synthesis deficiency syndromes marked by low brain creatine and neurodevelopmental impairment.

label: Glycine
description: Glycine serves as the second amino acid substrate for endogenous creatine synthesis. Arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) condenses arginine with glycine to produce guanidinoacetate (GAA), which is then methylated by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) using S-adenosyl methionine to yield creatine. Because glycine and arginine are the committed substrates for creatine biosynthesis, their availability influences the rate of endogenous creatine production, which normally covers about half of daily needs. The rest is obtained from dietary red meat, fish, or supplements, and total body creatine stores are typically around 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass.

label: DNA Methylation
description: Because endogenous creatine synthesis is the major consumer of methyl groups donated by S-adenosylmethionine, creatine status may influence DNA methylation reactions that govern gene expression, including the expression of oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Supplemental creatine, by reducing the requirement for de novo creatine synthesis, could preserve methyl groups for DNA methyltransferases and thereby modulate global DNA methylation patterns. The trace notes that this is an emerging and largely hypothesis-driven area: creatine's effects on DNA methylation and on one-carbon metabolism have been examined mainly in animal and small human studies, and any causal link to cancer prevention remains to be firmly established.

label: Cancer Metabolism
description: Creatine and the creatine kinase system are increasingly studied in the context of cancer metabolism. Some cancer types, particularly those with a poor prognosis, upregulate creatine kinase isoenzymes, and creatine metabolism has been reported to support the growth and invasiveness of certain tumors, whereas in other contexts creatine appears to restrain tumor growth, possibly through effects on energy homeostasis and AMPK. The trace explicitly notes that creatine's relationship to cancer is context-dependent and that current evidence is insufficient to recommend creatine as an anti-cancer intervention, underscoring the need for direct experimental studies.

label: Tumorigenesis
description: Emerging evidence reviewed in the source trace suggests creatine may exert direct anti-cancer effects, inhibiting tumorigenesis rather than only supporting athletic performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that creatine supplementation can raise cellular phosphocreatine and creatine kinase activity, and the resulting change in the cellular energy state, together with creatine-mediated effects on AMPK and anabolic signaling, may suppress cancer cell proliferation and transformation. Because cancer cells depend on high glycolytic flux and altered energy metabolism, interventions that perturb the creatine-phosphocreatine system are hypothesized to restrain tumor growth, although the trace stresses that much of this evidence is preliminary and requires confirmation in well-powered clinical studies.

label: AMPK
description: DHM activates AMPK, which synergistically raises NAD+ via NAMPT upregulation and thereby further potentiates SIRT3 activity. Directionally, DHM activates AMPK, which increases NAD+ to boost SIRT3. This dual SIRT3/AMPK engagement amplifies mitochondrial and metabolic defenses, protecting the liver and other tissues from metabolic and oxidative injury. It mirrors the indirect resveratrol cascade, suggesting convergent circuitry among polyphenols, and it illustrates how natural compounds often activate multiple, reinforcing pathways rather than a single target—an important consideration for interpreting their biological effects.

label: Muscle Wasting
description: Creatine supplementation has been investigated for its ability to attenuate muscle wasting in conditions of disuse, catabolism, and disease. In healthy subjects it amplifies the muscle gains from resistance training, and in some clinical populations, including elderly individuals and people with neuromuscular or catabolic diseases, creatine supplementation preserves lean mass and strength. Because cancer and its treatments frequently cause sarcopenia and cachexia, creatine's potential to blunt muscle loss is proposed as a supportive-care role for creatine in oncology, even if any direct anti-tumor effect remains unproven.

label: Ischemia-reperfusion Injury
description: Honokiol protects the brain against ischemia-reperfusion injury. Intravenous honokiol given 15 minutes before or 60 minutes after middle cerebral artery occlusion dose-dependently reduced infarct volume by 20-70% without significant hemodynamic changes. Protective mechanisms include inhibition of neutrophil infiltration and ROS production, suppression of post-ischemic glucose intolerance, disruption of the PSD95-nNOS interaction at the NMDA receptor complex (preventing calcium-dependent neurotoxic nitric oxide production), and suppression of glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production.

label: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
description: Preclinical studies suggest creatine supplementation can reduce the severity of spinal cord injury. Rats fed creatine before and after moderate spinal cord contusion developed less scar tissue and performed better on locomotor function tests than controls, and rats fed a 2% creatine diet before and after injury experienced less loss of gray matter. In humans with cervical spinal cord injury, creatine supplementation enhanced aerobic exercise capacity, ventilatory anaerobic threshold, and, combined with vitamin D and resistance training, improved arm muscle area, strength, and functional capacity. These findings support creatine as an adjunct that may reduce injury severity and enhance rehabilitation outcomes after spinal cord injury.

label: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
description: Creatine supplementation has shown neuroprotective potential in traumatic brain injury. In animal models, providing creatine in the diet for 5 days prior to TBI decreased cortical brain damage by 36% in rats and 50% in mice, an effect attributed to improved energy availability in the injured brain. Creatine also reduces the severity of mild concussions and ischemic brain damage and improves learning and memory during recovery in neonatal mice. While these preclinical studies cannot be replicated in humans, they support the contention that creatine supplementation may reduce the severity of TBI and serve as an adjunctive strategy in individuals at risk of head injury, complementing its established role in muscle and rehabilitation settings.

label: Neuroprotection
description: SIRT1 confers neuroprotection by deacetylating FOXO and PGC-1alpha to drive antioxidant and mitochondrial programs, suppressing NF-kB-mediated neuroinflammation, and promoting non-amyloidogenic APP processing via ADAM10; it protects against beta-amyloid toxicity and supports BDNF expression through Hes1 deacetylation.

label: ADP
description: Creatine provides the immediate phosphate group needed to recycle ADP back into ATP, the cellular energy currency, keeping cellular energy pools saturated and reducing metabolic stress, which protects HRV from plunging during hard training. It is recommended daily at 3-5 grams, ideally post-workout or with the largest carbohydrate meal, because creatine uptake is enhanced by insulin. Pairing creatine with carbohydrates and protein helps drive it into muscle and brain cells more efficiently, with consistency mattering more than exact timing.

label: Pro-inflammatory Cytokines
description: Creatine has immunomodulatory effects that include reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and other inflammatory markers like TNF-alpha and PGE2. A creatine-induced reduction of these inflammatory mediators may help explain some of the neuroprotective benefits observed in patients with central nervous system diseases and the attenuation of inflammatory and muscle damage markers after intense exercise. Creatine also down-regulates expression of toll-like receptors (TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, TLR-7) in a mouse macrophage cell line and may influence cytokines through the NF-kB signaling pathway, with potential consequences for immune response and, notably, for TLR-4-mediated pathology in Parkinson's disease progression.

label: ATP
description: The primary biochemical function of creatine is to buffer cellular ATP levels through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. Creatine kinase reversibly catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP at rates far exceeding mitochondrial or glycolytic ATP production, which is essential for short bursts of intense activity. The creatine kinase reaction therefore acts as a rapid temporal energy buffer, maintaining ATP:ADP ratios during muscle contraction and other energy-demanding processes. This ATP-regenerating capacity is the basis for creatine's ergogenic effects and is also central to hypotheses about its influence on cancer cell metabolism.

label: Creatine Kinase
description: The biological actions of creatine are mediated by the creatine kinase enzyme family, which catalyzes the reversible phosphorylation of creatine by ATP. Tissue-specific creatine kinase isoforms are expressed in muscle, brain, and other tissues, and the enzyme couples the phosphocreatine pool to cellular ATP demand. In tissues with high and fluctuating energy requirements, the creatine kinase reaction buffers ATP levels and transports high-energy phosphate between sites of production and consumption. Because creatine kinase is also expressed in several tumors, the enzyme is a candidate interface through which creatine supplementation could influence cancer cell energy metabolism.

label: Creatine Synthesis Deficiency
description: High-dose, long-term creatine supplementation is a nutritional strategy for creatine synthesis deficiencies caused by mutations in AGAT, GAMT, or the creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which reduce endogenous creatine synthesis or cellular uptake and result in low brain creatine and phosphocreatine. Supplementation at 0.3-0.8 g/kg/day increases brain creatine and PCr levels and improves or stabilizes clinical symptoms including intellectual disability, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Patients with GAMT or AGAT deficiency treated early (e.g., starting at four months of age) can experience normal psychomotor development, and such therapy is well tolerated and may also benefit ornithine aminotransferase deficiency causing gyrate atrophy.

label: Methyl groups
description: Creatine synthesis is the single largest consumer of S-adenosylmethionine-derived methyl groups in the body, using approximately 70 percent of available methyl donor flux. Guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate to form creatine, thereby competing with DNA methylation and other methylation reactions for the methyl pool. Because exogenous creatine supplementation reduces the demand for endogenous creatine synthesis, it can spare methyl groups and shift the balance of methylation reactions. This creatine-methionine interaction forms the mechanistic basis for the hypothesis that creatine could influence epigenetic processes relevant to cancer.

label: Creatine Kinase (CK)
description: Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

label: Adenosine Triphosphate
description: Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

label: CTPI2
source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
description: CTPI2 is a third-generation inhibitor of the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 with high binding affinity and specificity. CTPI2 treatment results in dose-dependent suppression of SASP components at transcript and protein levels without altering cell cycle regulators, HMGB1 localization, DNA damage foci or proliferation markers. It reduces global nuclear acetylation and H3K27ac at SASP loci and abolishes incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into histone acetylation, yet does not broadly impair mitochondrial function: OXPHOS gene expression, ATP production, coupling efficiency, mitochondrial ROS and morphology remain largely unchanged.

label: Healthspan
source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
description: The Guardians of Mammalian Healthspan review (Giblin, Skinner and Lombard 2014) concludes that mammalian sirtuins, especially SIRT1, SIRT3 and SIRT6, broadly suppress age-related pathologies and promote healthspan. Directionally, sirtuin activity sits upstream of preserved tissue function across organ systems. Consistent with this, increased SIRT1 or SIRT6 expression extends mouse lifespan, positioning the family as guardians of mammalian health rather than simple lifespan determinants. The review emphasizes that sirtuins oppose inflammation, metabolic decline, and cellular damage, making them attractive targets for interventions aimed at compressing late-life morbidity.

label: SLC25A1
source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
description: CTPI2 is a third-generation inhibitor of the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 with high binding affinity and specificity. CTPI2 treatment results in dose-dependent suppression of SASP components at transcript and protein levels without altering cell cycle regulators, HMGB1 localization, DNA damage foci or proliferation markers. It reduces global nuclear acetylation and H3K27ac at SASP loci and abolishes incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into histone acetylation, yet does not broadly impair mitochondrial function: OXPHOS gene expression, ATP production, coupling efficiency, mitochondrial ROS and morphology remain largely unchanged.

label: DELE1
description: OMA1 is a mitochondrial protease whose activity is markedly elevated following mitochondrial stress. Upon stress, OMA1 catalyzes the cleavage of DELE1 during the stage of mitochondrial protein import and processing, producing a smaller cytosolic form (DELE1-S) that accumulates in the cytosol. The OMA1-dependent cleavage is required for subsequent ISR activation. Notably, perturbations of protein import across the inner mitochondrial membrane produce cytosolic DELE1 accumulation independent of OMA1, and iron deficiency causes full-length DELE1 (DELE1-L) accumulation on the outer mitochondrial membrane that activates HRI without OMA1-mediated cleavage.

label: HRI
description: DELE1, previously identified as a poorly characterized mitochondrial protein from a yeast two-hybrid screen, was converged upon by two independent CRISPR-based screens as the mediator of mitochondrial stress signaling to the ISR. Under mitochondrial stress, the cleaved cytosolic fragment DELE1-S directly binds and activates the heme-regulated kinase HRI. Importantly, HRI activation by DELE1 was shown to be heme-independent, ruling out the classical heme-depletion mechanism. HRI activation in turn leads to eIF2alpha phosphorylation and downstream ATF4 induction, linking mitochondrial dysfunction to the integrated stress response.

label: Diabetes Mellitus
source_file: _document_ - Aminoguanidine An AGE Product Inhibitor  Antiaging Systems Articles.md
description: Diabetes mellitus is often seen as a form of accelerated aging, and the levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of their equivalent normal non-diabetics. Advanced glycation end products are increased in diabetes and play an important role in the development of diabetic complications. Aminoguanidine acts to bind to sugars, preventing them from binding to the lysine groups of proteins, and diabetic clinical trials with humans have highlighted its ability to prevent oxidative modification of LDL, inhibit atherosclerotic plaque formation, reduce albuminuria and delay end-stage renal disease.

label: DRP1
source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
description: In Parkinson's disease, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation of dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1), a mitochondrial fission protein implicated in pathological fragmentation, restores mitochondrial dynamics, protects against dopaminergic neuronal loss, and ameliorates motor deficits in murine models. SIRT3 concurrently scavenges ROS, preserves electron transport chain integrity, and promotes mitochondrial autophagy, attenuating neurodegeneration in midbrain dopaminergic populations.

label: Mitochondrial Fission
source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
description: Mitochondrial dynamics is the continuous remodeling of the cellular mitochondrial network through the two opposite but coordinated processes of fission and fusion, accompanied by mitophagy and ultrastructural reshaping of the inner and outer membranes. Fission divides a single mitochondrion into two daughter mitochondria and is driven by the dynamin-related GTPase DRP1 recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane by adaptor proteins. The balance between fission and fusion is tightly regulated by conserved GTPase proteins and must be maintained to support normal mitochondrial and cellular function.

label: Mitochondrial Fission Sites
source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md
description: DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to defined sites on the mitochondrial outer membrane, where division occurs. Its adaptor proteins, including MFF, FIS1, MID49, and MID51, serve as receptors that concentrate DRP1 at prospective fission sites, often at positions where mitochondria are already constricted or associated with the endoplasmic reticulum. In cultured cells, MFF recruits DRP1 to the majority of fission events, while MID49 and MID51 recruit DRP1 to mitochondria independently of MFF in certain conditions. Once concentrated, DRP1 oligomerizes into spirals that wrap around the tubule, and GTP hydrolysis drives the membrane constriction required for complete scission.

label: Alzheimer's Disease
source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
description: Biochemical evaluation of Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains demonstrates significantly increased DRP1 and FIS1 and reduced MFN1, MFN2 and OPA1 mRNA and protein levels, correlating with mitochondrial fragmentation and compromised neuronal energy production. Excessive mitochondrial fission interferes with OXPHOS complex assembly and cristae integrity, and S-nitrosylation of DRP1 induced by amyloid beta triggers mitochondrial fission and neuronal damage. Significantly increased DRP1 phosphorylation at Ser616 stimulates DRP1 translocation to mitochondria and fission activity in AD brain, and impaired axonal transport and reduced mitophagy accompany AD progression.

label: Epacadostat
description: Epacadostat is a small-molecule inhibitor of IDO1 tested in clinical trials as an immuno-oncology strategy, often in combination with checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1. These combinations aim to relieve IDO1-mediated immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment by blocking tryptophan depletion and kynurenine production, thereby restoring effector T cell function. However, results from such trials have been mixed, and challenges including isoform selectivity, compensatory pathways (TDO, IDO2), and context-specific effects have limited clinical success.

label: IDO1
description: IDO1 is a heme-containing, monomeric cytosolic enzyme (~45 kDa) encoded by the IDO1 gene on chromosome 8p11.21 that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in the kynurenine pathway (KP) of tryptophan catabolism. It oxidizes L-tryptophan (and other indoleamine substrates such as D-Trp, 5-hydroxy-Trp, tryptamine and serotonin) to N-formylkynurenine in an O2-dependent reaction. The mechanism involves a heme iron center that binds O2, reduction of inactive ferric heme to active ferrous form, and oxidative cleavage of the indole ring at the 2,3-position. The KP accounts for ~95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production.

label: Everolimus
source_file: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md
description: Everolimus, a rapamycin analog (rapalog), is FDA approved for anti-seizure therapy in tuberous sclerosis complex after many years of off-label use. The EXIST-3 multicenter phase III study evaluated adjunctive everolimus in patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy due to TSC and showed significant reduction in seizure frequency, with approximately 40% of patients in the high-dose group achieving at least a 50% reduction in seizures compared to only 15% in placebo. The success reflects TSC's clearly defined molecular etiology, with highly penetrant mutations driving mTOR hyperactivation making the pathway an actionable target.

label: Immune System
source_file: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md
description: Cancer evades Immune System. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The immune system surveys and eliminates nascent malignancies, a process tumors must subvert to establish and progress. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Immune System rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

label: TSC
source_file: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md
description: Everolimus, a rapamycin analog (rapalog), is FDA approved for anti-seizure therapy in tuberous sclerosis complex after many years of off-label use. The EXIST-3 multicenter phase III study evaluated adjunctive everolimus in patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy due to TSC and showed significant reduction in seizure frequency, with approximately 40% of patients in the high-dose group achieving at least a 50% reduction in seizures compared to only 15% in placebo. The success reflects TSC's clearly defined molecular etiology, with highly penetrant mutations driving mTOR hyperactivation making the pathway an actionable target.

label: Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption
description: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), also known as the afterburn effect, is the elevated oxygen consumption that persists after an exercise session and represents the energy expended in excess of resting values during recovery. EPOC accounts for a portion of the total energy cost of exercise beyond the exercise itself, typically contributing an additional 7-15 percent of the exercise energy cost depending on intensity and duration. Because EPOC elevates the metabolic rate for hours after training, it is often cited to justify high-intensity training for weight management, although Speakman's analysis argues that the quantitative contribution to total daily expenditure is smaller than commonly claimed.

label: Post-exercise Energy Expenditure
description: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), also known as the afterburn effect, is the elevated oxygen consumption that persists after an exercise session and represents the energy expended in excess of resting values during recovery. EPOC accounts for a portion of the total energy cost of exercise beyond the exercise itself, typically contributing an additional 7-15 percent of the exercise energy cost depending on intensity and duration. Because EPOC elevates the metabolic rate for hours after training, it is often cited to justify high-intensity training for weight management, although Speakman's analysis argues that the quantitative contribution to total daily expenditure is smaller than commonly claimed.

label: Resting Metabolic Rate
description: Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is the rate at which the body consumes energy while at rest, and it is the single largest component of total daily energy expenditure (TEE), typically accounting for about 60-70 percent of daily energy use. It is measured under standardized conditions of rest, thermal neutrality, and a fasting state. Because RMR dominates total daily energy expenditure, any change in RMR, such as the transient elevation caused by exercise, has a disproportionate impact on overall energy balance and, over time, on body weight regulation. The review by Speakman focuses on how exercise-induced alterations in RMR influence energy balance.

label: Total Daily Energy Expenditure
description: Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is the rate at which the body consumes energy while at rest, and it is the single largest component of total daily energy expenditure (TEE), typically accounting for about 60-70 percent of daily energy use. It is measured under standardized conditions of rest, thermal neutrality, and a fasting state. Because RMR dominates total daily energy expenditure, any change in RMR, such as the transient elevation caused by exercise, has a disproportionate impact on overall energy balance and, over time, on body weight regulation. The review by Speakman focuses on how exercise-induced alterations in RMR influence energy balance.

label: Physical Activity
description: Exercise is defined as planned, structured, and repetitive physical activity performed specifically to improve or maintain physical fitness, and it constitutes a subset of total physical activity, which also includes occupational activity, domestic activity, and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). In the energy balance framework of the Speakman review, exercise is the most flexible and controllable component of total daily energy expenditure, and its contribution to daily energy use is quantified through doubly labelled water studies. Because exercise is a voluntary component, it is the primary target of public-health interventions aimed at raising daily energy expenditure.

label: Appetite
description: An important conclusion of the Speakman review is that exercise does not reliably increase appetite, and that in many individuals appetite is suppressed both during and for a period after exercise, an effect that can persist for up to 24 hours in some protocols. This is counter to the common belief that increased exercise necessarily drives increased food intake. When exercise does raise energy intake, the increase is generally smaller than the energy cost of the exercise, so a net negative energy balance is usually achieved. These findings support the view that exercise contributes to weight control by raising expenditure without a fully compensatory increase in intake.

label: Mitohormesis
description: Mitohormesis is defined as the process by which mild mitochondrial stress triggers adaptive cellular responses that rewire metabolism, enhance protein-folding capacity, and remodel the redox environment, ultimately leaving cells less vulnerable to future stress. It is described as a subcellular form of the more general principle of hormesis, in which a mild, non-lethal perturbation induces protective adaptations. The review notes that these stress-induced alterations persist even after the stress is relieved, leaving the cell or tissue in a less vulnerable state, which is the defining hormetic feature applied specifically to the mitochondrion.

label: Fasting
description: Intermittent fasting and time-restricted feeding compress the eating window to 8-10 hours to allow a 14-16 hour daily fasting period, described as the simplest and most effective way to activate AMPK and mitophagy. Constant snacking and chronic overeating abolish the fasting-induced AMPK signal necessary for mitophagy. Fasting-induced mitochondrial recycling is a core mitohormetic mechanism, and stopping food intake at least 3-4 hours before sleep is highlighted as a key variable that instantly improves overnight HRV by allowing the body to focus entirely on cellular repair during sleep.

label: Fat Free Mass
description: Across and within individuals, resting metabolic rate (RMR) is most strongly predicted by fat free mass (FFM), which typically accounts for roughly 60-80 percent of the variance in RMR. Larger organs such as liver, brain, heart, and kidneys are metabolically expensive, so differences in lean mass drive most of the between-individual variation in RMR. Within a single individual, day-to-day variability of RMR is small, and the residual variability not explained by FFM includes fat mass, age, thyroid status, and ambient temperature. Because lean tissue is the primary metabolic driver, changes in muscle mass through training can modestly raise RMR.

label: Regulated Cell Death
source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
description: Ferroptosis is a regulated, iron-dependent cell death pathway in which cells lose their ability to regulate fats and eventually die, as distinct from unregulated necrotic death or other programmed death programs like apoptosis. It was discovered and named (originally 'oxytosis') by Pam Maher in 2001. The hallmark mechanism is accumulation of lipid peroxides to toxic levels, normally kept in check by glutathione, and the pathway is increasingly linked to neurodegeneration and age-related diseases. Because ferroptosis is druggable and genetically regulatable, it has become a promising therapeutic target alongside cellular senescence for supporting healthy aging and clearing dysfunctional cells.

label: FGF21
description: SIRT1 deacetylates PPARgamma, and this deacetylation promotes expression of FGF21 among a broader set of thermogenic and browning genes. Induction of FGF21, in turn, supports adipose tissue browning and increases energy expenditure, consistent with SIRT1's anti-obesity actions. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of PPARgamma deacetylation and FGF21 induction. FGF21 acts systemically to enhance glucose uptake, lipid oxidation, and adaptive thermogenesis, extending the effects of SIRT1 beyond the adipocyte itself.

label: Thermogenesis
description: FGF21 induces thermogenesis and promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent mechanisms. FGF21 promotes thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, with protein restriction stimulating WAT beiging via FGF21 action in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and PR similarly increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue via an FGF21-dependent mechanism. These effects drive the increased energy expenditure observed with protein restriction and contribute to its metabolic benefits including reduced body weight and adiposity despite increased food intake. FGF21 also regulates lipid homeostasis, reducing circulating triglycerides, and mediates PR effects on senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue.

label: Protein Restriction
description: Dietary protein restriction (PR) is a robust geroprotective regimen that extends lifespan in yeast, flies, and rodents and improves healthspan. Rodent studies demonstrate lifespan extension across many strains (for example, 34.9% in male C57BL/6J mice on a 21% vs 7% protein diet, and large extensions in flies), while restriction of specific essential amino acids - particularly methionine, isoleucine, and valine - recapitulates many of PR's benefits. FGF21-null mice do not live longer on PR, identifying FGF21 as essential for the longevity benefits. The Okinawan population's ~9% protein diet is cited as a human parallel to PR's lifespan effects.

label: FIS1
source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md
description: FIS1 is a tail-anchored outer mitochondrial membrane protein that functions as a receptor for DRP1, helping to recruit the fission machinery to mitochondria. In yeast, the FIS1 ortholog Fis1p is the main membrane anchor for the Dnm1p fission GTPase, whereas in mammalian cells FIS1 plays a more accessory role alongside MFF, MID49, and MID51, and may also mediate non-DRP1 functions such as recruiting proteasomal and autophagic machinery to mitochondria. Overexpression of FIS1 fragments mitochondria, whereas FIS1 knockdown produces elongated networks, confirming its pro-fission role, although its relative importance varies between cell types and conditions.

label: Fisetin
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a natural flavonoid of the flavonol subclass found in strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions, and cucumbers, with strawberries being the richest dietary source. It has the molecular formula C15H10O6 and a molecular weight of 286.24 g/mol. Fisetin is widely studied as a senolytic agent, and its anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, and neuroprotective activities are reported in numerous in vitro and in vivo studies. Despite its broad pharmacological potential, fisetin has extremely poor aqueous solubility, which severely limits its oral bioavailability.

label: Anti-oxidative Activity
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin is a potent antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species and stimulates endogenous antioxidant defenses including Nrf2-dependent expression of heme oxygenase-1, catalase, and superoxide dismutase. Its multiple hydroxyl groups allow it to donate electrons to quench free radicals and chelate metal ions that catalyze oxidative damage. The anti-oxidative action of fisetin underpins its protective effects in neuronal, cardiac, hepatic, and renal models of oxidative stress, and is considered a core mechanism shared with other polyphenols in its protective pharmacology.

label: Senolytic Activity
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin is among the most extensively studied naturally occurring senolytics. It selectively eliminates senescent cells by inhibiting key pro-survival pathways, including the PI3K/Akt and Bcl-xL pathways that senescent cells depend on to resist apoptosis. In aged mice, a short course of oral fisetin reduced senescent cell burden in multiple tissues, extended healthspan and median lifespan, and alleviated age-related dysfunction. This senolytic activity distinguishes fisetin from many flavonoids and has driven its evaluation in human clinical trials for osteoarthritis, frailty, and other age-related conditions, though pharmacokinetic limitations remain a central obstacle.

label: Anti-cancer Activity
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin shows broad anti-cancer activity against cell lines derived from lung, colon, breast, prostate, liver, melanoma, bladder, and leukemia. It inhibits cancer cell proliferation by arresting the cell cycle at G1 or G2/M phase, induces apoptosis through the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway with activation of caspases and modulation of Bcl-2 family proteins, and suppresses invasion and metastasis by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Fisetin also sensitizes tumor cells to conventional chemotherapeutics. Its anti-cancer efficacy in animal models, however, has been limited by the low concentrations achieved after oral dosing.

label: Anti-diabetic Activity
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin improves glucose homeostasis in experimental diabetes by enhancing insulin sensitivity and reducing hepatic glucose output. In diabetic rodents it lowers fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin, reduces insulin resistance, and protects pancreatic beta cells, in part through its antioxidant activity and activation of AMPK signaling in liver and muscle. The review notes these metabolic benefits depend on adequate systemic exposure, which the oral delivery of unformulated fisetin may not achieve, further emphasizing the need for bioavailability-improving formulations to realize its therapeutic potential in humans.

label: Limited Oral Absorption
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin is incompletely and variably absorbed after oral administration due to its low water solubility and rapid first-pass metabolism by intestinal and hepatic conjugating enzymes. Bioavailability studies report low and highly variable plasma fisetin concentrations after oral dosing, with most of the absorbed compound present as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates rather than the parent aglycone. The review identifies this limited oral absorption as the principal barrier to clinical translation of fisetin's broad preclinical pharmacology, and the majority of the formulation strategies it discusses are specifically aimed at increasing the fraction of the orally administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.

label: Low Water Solubility
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin has extremely low water solubility, reported in the range of a few micrograms per milliliter, which classifies it as a Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II or IV drug. The low solubility, combined with poor permeability in some assessments and extensive intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, results in low and erratic oral bioavailability. Because dissolution is the rate-limiting step for oral absorption, much of the formulation research described in the review aims to increase the dissolution rate and apparent solubility of fisetin, using approaches such as solid dispersions, cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, and nanocrystals.

label: Neuroprotective Activity
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin exerts neuroprotective effects that are attributed to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct signaling actions in neurons. It protects cultured neurons from oxidative and excitotoxic insults, and in animal models of ischemia and Parkinson's disease it reduces neuronal loss and improves motor function. Fisetin also acts as a cognitive enhancer, improving learning and memory in healthy rodents through modulation of ERK-CREB signaling and by promoting synaptic plasticity, and it has been proposed as a candidate for Alzheimer's disease based on its ability to reduce beta-amyloid aggregation and tau pathology. These effects motivate delivery strategies aimed at improving brain exposure.

label: Bcl-xL
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: MOMP is inhibited by Bcl-xL. Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) is the committed, largely irreversible step of intrinsic apoptosis that releases intermembrane-space proteins. Bcl-xL is an anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family protein that maintains mitochondrial integrity and is essential for platelet and many tumor-cell survival. The directionality runs from Bcl-xL toward MOMP, so Bcl-xL is the active agent and MOMP the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

label: Inflammation
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: SIRT6 suppresses inflammation by deacetylating H3K9 at NF-kB target-gene promoters and promoting p65 degradation, restraining pro-inflammatory transcription; loss of SIRT6 elevates inflammatory output and contributes to age-related inflammation.

label: Senolytic Agent
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin belongs to the pharmacological class of senolytics, agents that selectively kill senescent cells. Senolytics, exemplified by fisetin and dasatinib plus quercetin, exploit the reliance of senescent cells on anti-apoptotic survival networks. Fisetin's senolytic profile was identified in screening studies and validated in mouse models where it cleared senescent cells in adipose tissue, bone marrow, and other organs and extended healthspan. Because senescent cell accumulation drives tissue dysfunction and age-related disease, fisetin is now being evaluated in human trials, and its classification as a senolytic frames the therapeutic rationale for improving its bioavailability.

label: Flavonoids
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a natural flavonoid of the flavonol subclass found in strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions, and cucumbers, with strawberries being the richest dietary source. It has the molecular formula C15H10O6 and a molecular weight of 286.24 g/mol. Fisetin is widely studied as a senolytic agent, and its anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, and neuroprotective activities are reported in numerous in vitro and in vivo studies. Despite its broad pharmacological potential, fisetin has extremely poor aqueous solubility, which severely limits its oral bioavailability.

label: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: Once absorbed, fisetin is extensively conjugated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) and sulfotransferases in the intestinal epithelium and liver, producing fisetin glucuronide and fisetin sulfate metabolites that circulate in the plasma. Because these conjugates have reduced biological activity and are rapidly excreted via bile and urine, the parent aglycone fisetin reaches only low concentrations in tissues. The extent of this phase II metabolism is a primary cause of fisetin's poor oral bioavailability and short plasma half-life, and it is one reason most preclinical efficacy studies have used intraperitoneal injection rather than oral dosing.

label: PI3K/Akt
source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
description: PI3K/AKT signaling regulates Sirt3 in various contexts, generally opposing SIRT3-mediated catabolic/mitochondrial programs (e.g., PI3K/AKT modulates Sirt3 in activated microglia); Table 3 lists PI3K/AKT among negative regulators of the SIRT3 pathway (PMID 37930585).

label: FUNDC1
source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
description: FUNDC1 (FUN14 domain containing 1) is an outer mitochondrial membrane protein that serves as a mitophagy receptor for hypoxia-induced mitophagy, interacting directly with LC3 after dephosphorylation by phosphoglycerate mutase 5. ULK1 interacts with FUNDC1 and phosphorylates it at serine 17, enhancing FUNDC1 binding to LC3, and FUNDC1 interacts with OPA1 and DRP1 in a manner regulated by serine 13 phosphorylation during hypoxia or membrane potential loss. DRP1 can interact with overexpressed FUNDC1 to facilitate mitochondrial fragmentation and Parkin-mediated mitophagy.

label: GCN2
description: Protein restriction activates GCN2, an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive serine/threonine kinase triggered by amino acid restriction through uncharged tRNAs as well as by ribosome stalling and collision. Activated GCN2 phosphorylates eIF2alpha, suppressing global protein synthesis while selectively promoting translation of ATF4, a key activator of stress response and autophagy genes. Drosophila lacking Gcn2 die when amino acids are restricted, and deletion of Gcn2 in yeast blocks dietary restriction lifespan extension, while overexpression extends lifespan. During PR, GCN2 is initially required for FGF21 induction and also activates hepatic gluconeogenesis in response to decreased amino acid availability.

label: ATF4
description: ATF4 emerged as a common and critical downstream mediator of the metabolic reprogramming that occurs following diverse mitochondrial stressors in mammalian cells. Strategies including doxycycline inhibition of mitochondrial translation, actinonin-mediated destabilization of OXPHOS proteins, FCCP reduction of mitochondrial membrane potential, and MitoBloCK-6 impairment of protein import all converge on ATF4 induction through a conserved amino acid response element (AARE) in the promoters of metabolic response genes. Other mediators such as ATF5, p53, and c-Myc also participate in the broader mitochondrial stress transcriptional response.

label: Tryptophan
description: IDO1 is a heme-containing, monomeric cytosolic enzyme (~45 kDa) encoded by the IDO1 gene on chromosome 8p11.21 that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in the kynurenine pathway (KP) of tryptophan catabolism. It oxidizes L-tryptophan (and other indoleamine substrates such as D-Trp, 5-hydroxy-Trp, tryptamine and serotonin) to N-formylkynurenine in an O2-dependent reaction. The mechanism involves a heme iron center that binds O2, reduction of inactive ferric heme to active ferrous form, and oxidative cleavage of the indole ring at the 2,3-position. The KP accounts for ~95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production.

label: Ghrelin
description: The metabolic hormone ghrelin, a major regulator of food intake, also exerts immunomodulatory and thymopoietic effects. Ghrelin binds immune cell subsets via ghrelin-specific receptors and localizes to lipid rafts of activated T cells. Dixit et al. reported that ghrelin reduces age-associated inflammatory responses in mice, and in aged thymus both ghrelin and growth hormone levels decrease in correlation with functional thymic involution and elevated inflammation.

label: Thymopoiesis
description: The thymus is a vital organ for homeostatic maintenance of the peripheral immune system. Within its two compartments, the true thymic epithelial space (TES, comprising cortex and medulla) and the perivascular space (PVS), T cells develop, mature, and undergo induction of self-tolerance in a process called thymopoiesis. The cortex hosts early thymocyte development including T cell receptor gene rearrangement and positive selection, while the medulla carries out negative selection to remove autoreactive T cells. The perivascular space, composed of adipocytes, peripheral lymphocytes and stroma, is a non-thymopoietic component.

label: Glutathione
source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
description: Glutathione, an antioxidant, keeps lipid peroxides at steady levels and thereby staves off ferroptosis in healthy cells. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent cell death pathway in which the accumulation of lipid peroxides becomes toxic, and glutathione's antioxidant capacity is the canonical defense against this form of death. The Salk study's discovery is notable because the acid ceramidase axis sensitizes cells to ferroptosis without involving changes in glutathione levels, operating instead through lipid metabolism - an entirely novel, GPX4/GSH-independent pathway. This contrasts with the classical view that ferroptosis sensitivity is controlled chiefly by glutathione/GPX4-dependent peroxide neutralization.

label: Glycation
source_file: _document_ - Aminoguanidine An AGE Product Inhibitor  Antiaging Systems Articles.md
description: Glycation is the product of the reaction between a sugar and the free amino group of proteins, referred to as cross-linking, and the accumulation of these glycation byproducts results in large, cross-linked molecules that inhibit the ability of the cell to function normally. Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) accumulate with age in tissues, contributing to arterial stiffening and cardiac enlargement. Levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of non-diabetics, and AGEs are believed to play an important role in the development of diabetic complications.

label: HAF-1
description: HAF-1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane ABC-transporter family protein in C. elegans that exports matrix-derived peptides into the cytosol to signal mitochondrial stress. Proteins degraded by matrix proteases generate peptides that exit the mitochondria through HAF-1 (analogous to the yeast Mdl1 transporter), and this peptide release triggers a nuclear transcriptional response involving the ubiquitin-like protein UBL-5, the homeobox transcription factor DVE-1, and ATFS-1. The mechanism is reminiscent of peptide-based quorum sensing in gram-positive bacteria, where peptides exported via ABC transporters activate two-component histidine kinase sensors.

label: Mitochondrial Peptides
description: HAF-1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane ABC-transporter family protein in C. elegans that exports matrix-derived peptides into the cytosol to signal mitochondrial stress. Proteins degraded by matrix proteases generate peptides that exit the mitochondria through HAF-1 (analogous to the yeast Mdl1 transporter), and this peptide release triggers a nuclear transcriptional response involving the ubiquitin-like protein UBL-5, the homeobox transcription factor DVE-1, and ATFS-1. The mechanism is reminiscent of peptide-based quorum sensing in gram-positive bacteria, where peptides exported via ABC transporters activate two-component histidine kinase sensors.

label: Heart Rate Variability
description: HRV is directly controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which has two main branches with opposing effects. The sympathetic nervous system, the fight-flight-freeze system, releases adrenaline and cortisol that force the heart to beat faster and more rhythmically, lowering HRV. The parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-digest-and-repair system controlled heavily by the vagus nerve, allows more fluctuation between heartbeats, raising HRV. A high HRV therefore reflects strong vagal tone and a cardiovascular system that is highly responsive and flexible, while low HRV signals chronic stress, fatigue, or illness.

label: Autonomic Nervous System
description: HRV is directly controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which has two main branches with opposing effects. The sympathetic nervous system, the fight-flight-freeze system, releases adrenaline and cortisol that force the heart to beat faster and more rhythmically, lowering HRV. The parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-digest-and-repair system controlled heavily by the vagus nerve, allows more fluctuation between heartbeats, raising HRV. A high HRV therefore reflects strong vagal tone and a cardiovascular system that is highly responsive and flexible, while low HRV signals chronic stress, fatigue, or illness.

label: Honokiol
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol, a biphenolic lignan from Magnolia bark, physically interacts with SIRT3, increasing its deacetylase activity and upregulating SIRT3 protein expression. Directionally, honokiol sits upstream of SIRT3 activation. This engagement yields downstream deacetylation of mitochondrial antioxidant and metabolic targets, including MnSOD and OSCP. Honokiol thereby mimics caloric-restriction benefits specifically within mitochondria, and its effects are lost when SIRT3 is knocked down, confirming SIRT3 dependence. Because honokiol is lipophilic and poorly water-soluble, its formulation and delivery are practical considerations for therapeutic use.

label: Akt
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Akt signaling is associated with inhibition of SIRT2-dependent cell-cycle and stress outputs (e.g., cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylates SIRT2 at Ser331 to reduce its deacetylase activity), placing AKT signaling among negative regulators of the SIRT2 pathway (Pandithage et al., 2008, J Cell Biol, PMID 18504304).

label: Inflammatory Pain
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol attenuates inflammatory pain, reducing formalin-induced paw-licking behavior in the inflammatory phase and thermal hyperalgesia in mice. It blocks nociceptive signaling evoked by NMDA, glutamate, substance P, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in superficial laminae (I-II) of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn. Compared with magnolol, honokiol is more selective for NMDA-induced behavioral responses and hyperalgesia. Its analgesic effects are multifactorial, involving both the inflammatory cascade and glutamatergic/NMDA receptor pathways.

label: Neuronal Death
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: While honokiol is neuroprotective at low doses, it increases neuronal death in vitro at higher concentrations: 100 uM applied directly to fetal cortical neurons is toxic. This dose-dependent biphasic behavior underscores the need to define human pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters before clinical administration. The potential neurotoxicity at supraphysiological concentrations, combined with honokiol's antithrombotic activity, highlights the importance of careful dosing and patient selection for any therapeutic use.

label: Blood-Brain Barrier
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol, a lipid-soluble lignan extracted from Magnolia species, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier to exert its effects in the central nervous system, including anti-tumorigenic and neuroprotective actions. Its lipid solubility allows it to pass lipid bilayers and act at multiple intracellular and membrane sites, a property shared with the structurally related anesthetic propofol and the analog magnolol. BBB penetration is a prerequisite for honokiol's anxiolytic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-seizure activities in the brain.

label: Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol increases the activity of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), the enzyme responsible for GABA synthesis, in the cortex and hippocampus of mice. By enhancing GAD(65) and GAD(67) activity, honokiol can augment the brain's synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, which may complement its direct positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors. This combined effect on GABAergic tone is consistent with honokiol's central depressant, anticonvulsant, anxiolytic, and sleep-promoting pharmacological profile.

label: Arterial Thrombosis
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol is a potent inhibitor of arterial thrombosis, acting through endothelial cell protection and stimulation of prostacyclin production. This antithrombotic effect is a safety consideration: caution is advised in coagulopathic patients, those with hemorrhagic stroke or hemorrhagic transformation after ischemic stroke, patients on warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin, and individuals with clotting disorders such as hemophilia or von Willebrand's deficiency. The bleeding risk must be weighed against honokiol's neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory benefits before clinical use.

label: Caspase-3
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Caspase-3 cleaves PARP1 at the DEVD↓G site during apoptosis, inactivating its DNA-repair capacity and conserving ATP for the death program. Directionally, caspase-3 sits upstream of PARP1 inactivation. This marks the point of irreversible commitment to apoptosis and is a classic biochemical marker of apoptotic execution. Because PARP1 is a major NAD+ consumer, its cleavage during apoptosis also spares NAD+ from repair-dependent depletion. The cleavage of PARP1 is widely used experimentally to detect apoptosis, and its regulation is relevant to both normal cell turnover and cancer therapy.

label: Neutrophils
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol inhibits neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, as measured by luminol-amplified chemiluminescence in neutrophils. By reducing the accumulation and oxidative burst of neutrophils at the site of ischemic injury, honokiol limits secondary tissue damage following stroke. This anti-inflammatory action is complemented by inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production, together contributing to honokiol's ability to reduce infarct volume in focal cerebral ischemia-reperfusion models.

label: NMDA receptor
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol inhibits NMDA-evoked cationic influx, blocking excessive calcium entry that would otherwise drive excitotoxic neuronal injury and seizures. In rat cerebellar granule cells, honokiol inhibited repetitive firing by blocking glutamate-, NMDA-, and K+-evoked cation influx, and intraperitoneal honokiol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure thresholds in NMDA-infusion models, being more potent than magnolol. In ischemic conditions honokiol also disrupts PSD95-nNOS coupling at the NMDA receptor postsynaptic complex, preventing neurotoxic nitric oxide production downstream of NMDA receptor activation.

label: Diazepam
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: In animal behavioral models, honokiol produces anxiolysis at doses as low as 0.2 mg/kg with fewer motor and cognitive side effects than the benzodiazepine diazepam. The anxiolytic effect of honokiol is blocked by flumazenil, bicuculline, CCK-4, and caffeine, whereas these agents differentially affect diazepam's anxiolysis (e.g., caffeine enhances diazepam's effect), suggesting honokiol may act through partly alternative pathways in addition to GABA-A potentiation. This favorable side-effect profile is a key rationale for developing honokiol as an anxiolytic.

label: GABA_A receptor
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol is a positive allosteric modulator of both synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors, a known target of benzodiazepines and other anxiolytics. It shows markedly higher efficacy at receptors containing the delta subunit (900-1100% response) compared with alpha-beta-gamma-only receptors (300-500%), and it allosterically increases the affinity of low-affinity sites, increasing [3H]muscimol binding about three-fold. This GABA-A modulation underpins honokiol's anxiolytic, hypnotic, and anticonvulsant properties and is the basis of its sleep-promoting effects via the benzodiazepine site.

label: Mitochondria
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: SIRT3 is the principal mitochondrial sirtuin, imported into the matrix where it removes acetyl, succinyl, and other acyl modifications from respiratory-chain and metabolic enzymes. Its activity is governed by the mitochondrial NAD+/NADH ratio, which links the cell's energy state directly to enzyme function, so SIRT3 serves as a metabolic sensor within the organelle. Because of its mitochondrial residence, SIRT3 is positioned to sense and tune local metabolism, driving oxidative phosphorylation, antioxidant defense, and fatty-acid oxidation.

label: Sodium Potassium ATPase
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol exerts neuroprotection in part by preserving the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase, the membrane pump critical for maintaining neuronal resting potential and ion homeostasis. In mouse models of cerebral ischemia, honokiol treatment preserved Na+/K+-ATPase activity and enzymatic mitochondrial function, correlating with reduced neuronal damage. Together with phosphorylation of pro-survival factors, preservation of mitochondrial function, and GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation is one of at least five distinct parallel mechanisms through which honokiol protects neurons from ischemic and oxidative injury.

label: Non-REM Sleep
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol promotes non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and shortens sleep latency. In mouse studies, honokiol at 10 and 20 mg/kg significantly decreased sleep latency and increased the amount of NREM sleep without affecting REM sleep or EEG power density, and it excited sleep-promoting neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area. These effects occur through the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. The combined sleep-promoting and anxiolytic actions suggest a potential role for honokiol as an anesthetic adjunct.

label: Amyloid Beta
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol significantly decreased beta-amyloid (Abeta)-induced neuronal death in neuronal culture models of Alzheimer's disease. In screening nine compounds from Chinese herbs for anti-Alzheimer's activity, only honokiol and magnolol markedly reduced Abeta-induced cell death. The protective mechanism involves decreased ROS production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of caspase-3 activity. A honokiol-containing extract of Magnolia officinalis also prevented lipopolysaccharide-induced memory deficiency via antineuroinflammatory and antiamyloidogenic effects, supporting honokiol's therapeutic potential in Alzheimer's disease.

label: Stroke
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol reduces cerebral infarction in rodent stroke models, including both pre-ischemic and post-ischemic administration paradigms. In MCA occlusion models, intravenous honokiol significantly reduced total infarct volume without creating significant hemodynamic changes. The neuroprotection is multifactorial, involving inhibition of neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production, suppression of post-ischemic glucose intolerance, disruption of PSD95-nNOS coupling to prevent neurotoxic nitric oxide generation, and inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and inflammatory cytokine production during ischemia-reperfusion.

label: Epilepsy
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol and its structural analog magnolol have been evaluated as potential therapies for epilepsy and related seizure disorders. Intraperitoneal injections of honokiol or magnolol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure threshold in mice challenged with intravenous NMDA, with honokiol appearing more potent than magnolol. Honokiol also ameliorated the behavioral and neurotoxic impairments induced by NMDA injection into the cerebral ventricular system, showing augmented neuroprotection compared with tea polyphenol or memantine alone, supporting a role for honokiol in seizure prevention.

label: c-Fos
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in the superficial (I-II) laminae of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn in mice, a marker of spinal nociceptive neuron activation. Along with reducing formalin-induced paw-licking, this shows honokiol acts at the spinal level to dampen pain transmission during the inflammatory phase of the formalin model. Honokiol's ability to suppress dorsal-horn c-Fos parallels its blockade of NMDA-, glutamate-, substance P-, and PGE2-evoked nociception, supporting a spinal component to its analgesic activity.

label: TNF-alpha
source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
description: Honokiol reduces TNF-alpha secretion from LPS-stimulated mouse macrophages. Using lipopolysaccharide to induce inflammation, honokiol decreased tumor necrosis factor-alpha secretion, inhibited nitric oxide expression, blocked protein kinase C-alpha membrane translocation, and suppressed NF-kappaB activation in macrophages, with similar anti-inflammatory effects translated to human monocyte-derived dendritic cells. By dampening this central pro-inflammatory cytokine, honokiol mitigates the inflammatory cascade that drives neuroinflammation and inflammatory pain, making it a candidate adjunct for inflammatory conditions.

label: Hormesis
description: Mitohormesis is defined as the process by which mild mitochondrial stress triggers adaptive cellular responses that rewire metabolism, enhance protein-folding capacity, and remodel the redox environment, ultimately leaving cells less vulnerable to future stress. It is described as a subcellular form of the more general principle of hormesis, in which a mild, non-lethal perturbation induces protective adaptations. The review notes that these stress-induced alterations persist even after the stress is relieved, leaving the cell or tissue in a less vulnerable state, which is the defining hormetic feature applied specifically to the mitochondrion.

label: Incoherent Bivalent Motif
description: Atypical dose-response curves where a drug's effect does not follow a monotonic shape are referred to as hormetic or biphasic. This computational study shows that all hormetic networks share a similar core structure: an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target of the drug, in which the two interactions emanating from the target have net opposite (direct or indirect) effects over the downstream output. Around 18% of all three-node network topologies contain this motif, and topologies with an incoherent bivalent motif show a roughly five-fold increased probability of exhibiting hormesis compared with all topologies.

label: Network Motif
description: The study screened 5346 possible three-node network topologies of a coarse-grained signaling cascade model using a high-throughput computational approach, with 5000 parameter sets and 30 inhibitor concentrations per topology. More than 500 topologies show clear non-monotonic dose-response curves, and hormesis is favored in networks with a high number of repressing interactions on average, with the highest fraction of hormetic parameter sets in a topology composed of four repressing interactions. The probability of hormesis increases as the network becomes more complex, indicating it depends on the density and complexity of the network.

label: ATM
description: HSPA8 (HSC70), a member of the heat shock protein 70 family, directly binds phosphorylated ATM, as shown by p-ATM-mediated co-immunoprecipitation, and this interaction is specifically attenuated by apigenin treatment. ATM is the central modulator of the DNA damage response whose activation drives a persistent SASP; the HSPA8-ATM crosstalk represents an upstream transduction step in the transition from the acute stress-associated phenotype to the full SASP.

label: p38 MAPK
description: p38 MAPK phosphorylates caspase-3 at Ser150, suppressing its proteolytic activity; this inhibition is reversed by the phosphatase PP2A. Directionally, p38 sits upstream of caspase-3 inhibition. This provides a survival signal that tempers apoptosis under certain stresses, and it shows that stress kinases can directly restrain executioner caspases. By phosphorylating pro-caspase-3, p38 reduces the pool available for proteolytic activation, blunting the death response. This regulatory layer illustrates how the balance between kinases and phosphatases determines the threshold for apoptotic commitment under stress.

label: Human Growth Hormone
description: Human growth hormone (HGH) is widely used for rejuvenation and longevity, yet it actually accelerates aging and shortens lifespan. Growth hormone is a pro-aging hormone because it indirectly activates mTOR, and the hype around growth hormone is based on a single publication that misinterpreted its acute effects. Unlike HGH, the anti-aging effects of rapamycin are not based on a single paper or a wild guess but on the work of thousands of scientists studying mTOR and its inhibitors in diverse organisms from yeast to humans.

label: IGF1
description: Growth hormone (GH) is a peptide hormone that impacts the immune system via its stimulatory effects on insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Hematopoietic cells can produce GH that indirectly promotes immune reconstitution via IGF-1 production, and IGF-1 provides anti-apoptotic signals and promotes immune cell survival. IGF-1 may also act directly on thymic stromal cells as a component of the thymus microenvironment cross-talk network and stimulate IL-7 production, and intrathymic IL-7 in turn promotes and regulates T cell survival and function.

label: Humanin
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: Humanin is the first small peptide of a putative set of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), a novel concept that challenges the traditional view of mitochondria as passive end-function organelles. It was discovered in 2001 by screening a cDNA library from the surviving fraction of an Alzheimer's disease patient brain for clones protecting neuronal cells from cell death induced by APP mutants, and identified as a 75bp open reading frame yielding a 24 amino acid peptide encoded within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA. Humanin is a harbinger of additional MDPs, as numerous putative ORFs are dispersed throughout the mitochondrial genome.

label: FPRL1
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: FPRL1, a seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor, was the first humanin receptor to be described. Humanin acts as an agonist for FPRL1 by inducing Ca2+ mobilization and rapid activation of ERK1/2 signaling, a commonly induced downstream pathway of G-protein-coupled receptors. In neuroblasts, both the 42-aa form of beta-amyloid peptide and humanin activate FPRL1, but only Abeta42 is cytotoxic, and this cytotoxicity is reversed by humanin, suggesting that the neuroprotective effects of humanin might be accomplished by competitively binding to FPRL1, which may contribute to its cytoprotective aspects.

label: BAX
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: Pro-apoptotic Bax opposes SIRT4's anti-apoptotic effects on mitochondria; under stress Bax-mediated mitochondrial permeabilization is associated with decreased SIRT4-mediated protection, so Bax is listed among negative regulators of SIRT4 in Table 3.

label: IGFBP3
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: A second group cloned humanin using a yeast two-hybrid screen as a partner of IGFBP3, and demonstrated that humanin binds to IGFBP3 with high affinity and specificity. IGFBP3 regulates IGF bioactivity and also induces apoptosis and inhibits cell growth independently of IGFs, and humanin protects against IGFBP3-induced apoptosis. Humanin does not interfere with IGF-I/IGFBP-3 binding but appears to bind to the heparin-binding domain of IGFBP-3, and a single amino acid substitution of alanine for phenylalanine at position 6 (F6AHN) abrogates IGFBP-3 binding.

label: Insulin Sensitivity
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: Administration of adiponectin to obese, high-fat-fed mice improves insulin sensitivity and lowers blood glucose, reflecting its role as an insulin-sensitizing adipokine. It acts through the AdipoR1/2 receptors to activate AMPK and PPAR-α pathways that enhance fatty-acid oxidation and glucose uptake. Directionally, adiponectin sits upstream of improved insulin action in peripheral tissues. Because SIRT1 raises adiponectin via the FOXO1–C/EBPα axis, this forms part of SIRT1's anti-diabetic circuitry, and declining adiponectin with obesity contributes to the insulin resistance that sirtuin-activating interventions aim to reverse.

label: Mitochondrial-Derived Peptide
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: Humanin is the first small peptide of a putative set of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), a novel concept that challenges the traditional view of mitochondria as passive end-function organelles. It was discovered in 2001 by screening a cDNA library from the surviving fraction of an Alzheimer's disease patient brain for clones protecting neuronal cells from cell death induced by APP mutants, and identified as a 75bp open reading frame yielding a 24 amino acid peptide encoded within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA. Humanin is a harbinger of additional MDPs, as numerous putative ORFs are dispersed throughout the mitochondrial genome.

label: Retrograde Signaling
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: Mitochondria communicate back to the cell through processes collectively referred to as retrograde signaling, and traditionally described means include Ca2+, cytochrome c, and ROS. Mitochondrial-derived peptides such as humanin are recently identified retrograde signals that are unique in that they are encoded within the mitochondrial genome sequences, unlike other retrograde molecules which are nuclear-encoded. Humanin functions as both an endocrine factor and an intracellular survival factor with several biological roles regulating cell survival and metabolism, and retrograde signaling is a biological process well conserved from simple yeast to humans.

label: Mitokines
description: Humanin is a peptide of approximately 24 amino acids believed to derive from a short, cryptic open reading frame within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA gene, and it was the first identified mammalian mitokine. Originally isolated as a protective factor against familial Alzheimer's disease, humanin circulates in plasma and exerts cytoprotective and metabolic effects in various experimental paradigms. It is considered the founding member of a class of mitochondrially-derived peptides (MDPs) causing systemic effects in mammals.

label: Mitochondrial DNA
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: In senescence and ageing, mitochondrial dysfunction promotes the cytosolic release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which activates cGAS-STING signalling and drives inflammatory responses and the SASP. Cytosolic mtDNA levels were unchanged in senescent MRC5 and IMR90 fibroblasts following SLC25A1 inhibition, indicating that metabolic regulation of histone acetylation restrains SASP independently of mtDNA release. STING inhibition with SN011 suppresses SASP gene expression without affecting histone acetylation, showing that mtDNA-driven innate immune signalling and mitochondrial control of histone acetylation are independent but complementary inputs that converge to enable full SASP expression.

label: Cells
source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
description: The humanin peptide sequence has been proposed to contain a pseudo-signal peptide, and when transfected into neuronal cells humanin is detected in the culture medium, indicating a secretory capacity that is blocked by inhibition of ER-golgi transport processes.
