source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Caspase activation, hallmark of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, is antagonistic to SIRT4's mitochondrial anti-apoptotic function; during apoptosis caspases cleave/deregulate mitochondrial effectors, placing caspases among negative regulators of the SIRT4 pathway (Table 3).

label: Fatty acid oxidation
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: SIRT5 activates fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (VLCAD, LCAD, MCAD, ECHA) via desuccinylation, supporting lipid catabolism during fasting; SIRT5 deficiency impairs fatty-acid metabolism and lowers ATP.

label: PPARγ
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: SIRT4 represses signaling by the nuclear receptor PPARalpha and destabilizes the mitochondrial trifunctional protein alpha (MTPalpha) subunit in hepatocytes. Together these actions shift liver metabolism away from mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation and toward anabolic lipid conservation. Directionally, SIRT4 sits upstream of suppressed fatty-acid utilization, positioning it as a metabolic brake that opposes the fatty-acid-catabolic programs promoted by SIRT3 and SIRT5. In nutrient-replete conditions this restrains wasteful fat burning, but under energetic stress it can limit the capacity to oxidize fatty acids, and this SIRT3/SIRT4 balance governs mitochondrial fuel choice.

label: LKB1
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: SIRT1 deacetylates LKB1, triggering its translocation from nucleus to cytoplasm where it phosphorylates and activates AMPK, alleviating oxidative stress. Because LKB1 is the master upstream AMPK kinase, SIRT1-dependent LKB1 relocalization is a key route by which sirtuin activity engages the energy sensor, reinforcing the SIRT1-AMPK reciprocal loop and linking sirtuin signaling to AMPK-dependent catabolism, autophagy, and mitochondrial biogenesis. The relationship is context-dependent, reflecting reciprocal regulation of the energy-sensing axes.

label: muscle protein synthesis
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Accumulating evidence suggests that urolithin A may promote muscle protein synthesis and muscle growth through various pathways. It can increase the rate of protein synthesis within muscle cells while inhibiting protein degradation processes, allowing muscle cells to more effectively synthesize new proteins and maintain muscle mass. This anabolic action, combined with enhanced mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, supports muscle hypertrophy, the maintenance of muscle mass, and improved recovery after exercise.

label: TLR3/TRIF signaling
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: The literature indicates that urolithin A blocks the NF-κB/STAT1 axis through the inactivation of TLR3/TRIF signaling, reducing inflammation and enhancing antioxidant defense. TLR3/TRIF is an upstream innate immune signaling route whose inactivation dampens downstream NF-κB activation and the production of inflammatory mediators. This mechanism contributes to urolithin A's anti-inflammatory activity in settings such as poly(I:C)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and supports its role in muscle recovery and protection from inflammation-induced damage.

label: FOXO
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: SIRT2 activates FOXO via deacetylation (e.g., FOXO, c-Myc, G6PD, PEPCK), influencing transcription, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and redox balance.

label: muscle protein degradation
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: The FoxO (forkhead box O) family is a group of transcription factors involved in regulating the synthesis and degradation of muscle proteins. Under catabolic conditions, nuclear FoxO drives expression of atrophy-related genes and activates specific protein degradation pathways that break down muscle proteins. Urolithin A suppresses FoxO activation, primarily by inhibiting its nuclear activity and reducing its regulation of these degradation pathways, thereby attenuating muscle protein degradation and helping to preserve muscle mass.

label: Ubiquitin-Proteasome System
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: The ubiquitin-proteasome system stands as one of the main pathways responsible for the degradation of intracellular proteins, including muscle proteins. Studies have found that urolithin A can attenuate the degradation of muscle proteins by inhibiting the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, possibly by influencing the activity of specific ubiquitin ligases or proteasomes. This inhibition contributes to urolithin A's muscle-sparing and anti-atrophic effects, helping to preserve muscle mass during catabolic states.

label: Atrogin-1
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 (muscle-specific RING finger protein 1 and 2) are pivotal molecules involved in muscle protein synthesis and degradation, functioning as muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases that drive protein breakdown during atrophy. Studies have shown that urolithin A can regulate muscle protein synthesis and degradation by inhibiting the activity of mTORC1 and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, thereby reducing atrophy signaling, attenuating protein degradation, and preserving muscle mass.

label: MuRF1
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: MuRF1 (muscle-specific RING finger protein 1) is a muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligase that, together with Atrogin-1, marks muscle proteins for ubiquitin-proteasome degradation during atrophy. Studies have shown that urolithin A can regulate muscle protein synthesis and degradation by inhibiting the activity of mTORC1 and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, thereby reducing muscle protein degradation and supporting the maintenance of muscle mass under catabolic conditions. Suppressing this E3 ligase reduces ubiquitination of muscle proteins and complements urolithin A's anabolic effects on protein synthesis.

label: Muscle Hypertrophy
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Urolithin A may have a positive impact on muscle hypertrophy and maintenance of muscle mass through multiple pathways, including promotion of muscle cell repair and growth, enhancement of mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and regulation of protein synthesis and degradation processes. It can increase the cross-sectional area of muscle fibers, muscle protein content, and muscle strength, thus promoting muscle hypertrophy. Current research is still limited and mostly conducted in vitro or in animal experiments, so human studies are needed.

label: Muscle Atrophy
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: In pathological conditions characterized by muscle atrophy, such as certain neuromuscular diseases or extended periods of immobility, urolithin A may offer potential benefits. It can stimulate muscle protein synthesis while inhibiting protein degradation pathways, including FoxO signaling, the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, helping to preserve muscle mass and mitigate muscle wasting. Human clinical validation of these anti-atrophic effects remains limited, but the mechanistic evidence is supportive.

label: ATP synthesis
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Urolithin A can promote the formation and enhanced function of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, thereby improving the synthesis rate of ATP in muscle cells. ATP is the primary energy molecule for muscle cells and is crucial for muscle contraction and exercise performance. By promoting mitochondrial function and muscle energy metabolism, urolithin A increases the energy supply to muscle cells, improving endurance, strength, and recovery, and providing sustained energy support during prolonged or high-intensity exercise.

label: muscle fatigue
source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
description: Existing evidence suggests that urolithin A may have a positive role in improving endurance and delaying muscle fatigue, both of which are intricately linked to mitochondrial function. By enhancing mitochondrial activity and ATP synthesis, urolithin A provides sustained energy support during prolonged or high-intensity exercise, and its anti-inflammatory properties alleviate tissue damage and muscle soreness caused by inflammation. Most studies have been conducted in vitro or on animals, so more human studies are needed to validate these effects.

label: Persulfates
description: Ammonium persulfate is one of the suitable persulfate oxidizing agents for converting adrenaline into adrenochrome, together with potassium persulfate and sodium persulfate. Sodium and ammonium persulfates are preferred over potassium persulfate for their good solubility in water. In the examples, ammonium persulfate (about 0.42 mole) is used with a sodium hydrogencarbonate buffer and a bismuth salt catalyst at 0 to 5 degrees C to produce adrenochrome in maximum yield within about 30 to 45 minutes.

label: Bismuth
description: Water-soluble salts of bismuth, such as bismuth nitrate, bismuth oxynitrate, bismuth oxycarbonate, and bismuth citrate, accelerate the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, producing high-quality adrenochrome in high yields in a short period of time (about 30 to 45 minutes). Bismuth salts are used in amounts of 0.001 to 0.01 mole per mole of adrenaline; amounts below this do not significantly increase the reaction rate, while amounts above 0.01 mole may cause excessive oxidation and decompose the adrenochrome into tar-like by-products.

label: adrenochrome synthesis
description: Water-soluble salts of bismuth, such as bismuth nitrate, bismuth oxynitrate, bismuth oxycarbonate, and bismuth citrate, accelerate the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, producing high-quality adrenochrome in high yields in a short period of time (about 30 to 45 minutes). Bismuth salts are used in amounts of 0.001 to 0.01 mole per mole of adrenaline; amounts below this do not significantly increase the reaction rate, while amounts above 0.01 mole may cause excessive oxidation and decompose the adrenochrome into tar-like by-products.

label: Potassium ferricyanide
description: Adrenochrome has been commercially prepared by oxidizing adrenaline or its salts with potassium ferricyanide in an aqueous medium. This process is uneconomical because of the large quantities of potassium ferricyanide needed, the ensuing effluent disposal problems, and variability in product quality. The patent presents a bismuth-catalyzed persulfate process as a superior alternative that precludes these problems and yields less-colored carbazochrome and adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine products.

label: Hydrazines
description: Adrenochrome is very unstable due to its ortho-quinoid structure and is therefore usually stabilized by conventional derivatization with hydrazines, e.g., aminoguanidine, semicarbazide, phenylhydrazine, o-nitrophenylhydrazine, p-nitrophenylhydrazine, and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. These hydrazine derivatives serve both for the stabilization of adrenochrome and for the preparation of useful medicines such as hemostatics. The stabilization treatment is generally conducted for 30 minutes to 3 hours at a temperature of 0 to 15 degrees C.

label: Semicarbazide
description: Semicarbazide reacts with adrenochrome to form adrenochrome monosemicarbazone (carbazochrome), a hemostatic agent. In the patented process, semicarbazide hydrochloride is added to the adrenochrome solution at below 10 degrees C in the presence of a potassium acetate buffer, with the stabilization carried out at pH 5 to 7. The reaction yields about 40.0 g of crude powder that is purified by dissolving in dilute sodium hydroxide, active carbon treatment, and precipitation at pH 5.5, and the purified product shows an ultraviolet absorption maximum at 354 nm and characteristic infrared absorptions matching those of an authentic sample.

label: Sodium hydrogencarbonate
description: The aqueous reaction medium for adrenochrome synthesis is maintained at a pH from 4 to 8, preferably with a buffer such as sodium hydrogencarbonate, sodium dihydrogenphosphate, disodium hydrogenphosphate, potassium acetate, or sodium acetate, with sodium hydrogencarbonate being preferred. The buffer is generally used in an amount of 4 to 7 moles, preferably 5 to 6 moles, per mole of adrenaline. Maintaining this pH range supports the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline catalyzed by water-soluble bismuth salts.

label: Ammonium Persulfate
description: Ammonium persulfate is one of the suitable persulfate oxidizing agents for converting adrenaline into adrenochrome, together with potassium persulfate and sodium persulfate. Sodium and ammonium persulfates are preferred over potassium persulfate for their good solubility in water. In the examples, ammonium persulfate (about 0.42 mole) is used with a sodium hydrogencarbonate buffer and a bismuth salt catalyst at 0 to 5 degrees C to produce adrenochrome in maximum yield within about 30 to 45 minutes.

label: 495 nm wavelength
description: During the oxidation of adrenaline, the reaction mixture is tinged with purplish red due to the production of adrenochrome, and its color becomes deeper with increasing adrenochrome content. The reaction is continued until the absorbance at a wavelength of 495 nm, measured by sampling the reaction mixture at an appropriate time, reaches a maximum, at which point further oxidation of the product is minimized and adrenochrome is obtained in maximum yield. The reaction time required for maximum yield varies from 30 to 45 minutes depending on the temperature of the reaction mixture and the level of catalyst employed.

label: Yoshinori Ohsumi
description: Yoshinori Ohsumi was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his pioneering work using yeast genetics to identify the core autophagy-related (ATG) genes that govern the process. Through systematic mutagenesis screens, he uncovered the molecular machinery responsible for autophagosome formation, including the ubiquitin-like conjugation systems that build the phagophore membrane. His discoveries established autophagy as a genetically tractable and evolutionarily conserved degradation pathway, providing the conceptual framework for all subsequent mammalian autophagy research. The recognition underscored the fundamental importance of autophagy in cellular homeostasis, development, and human disease.

label: Lysosomal catabolic process
description: Autophagy is a conserved lysosome-dependent catabolic process in which cytoplasmic constituents—including misfolded proteins, protein aggregates, damaged organelles, and intracellular pathogens—are sequestered into double-membrane autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for enzymatic degradation. The resulting macromolecular building blocks such as amino acids, fatty acids, and nucleotides are recycled to sustain metabolism and biosynthetic capacity during nutrient stress. As the cell's principal quality-control and nutrient-recycling system, autophagy is essential for maintaining proteostasis and organellar integrity across nearly all eukaryotic cells. Defects in autophagic flux are causally linked to aging, neurodegeneration, cancer, and metabolic disease, making it a central node in cellular homeostasis.

label: Macroautophagy
description: Macroautophagy (commonly termed autophagy) is the best-characterized form, in which a de novo formed double-membrane structure called the phagophore expands to engulf cytoplasmic cargo and seals into an autophagosome. The autophagosome then fuses with a lysosome, forming an autolysosome where luminal contents are degraded by acidic hydrolases. This bulk and selective degradative route is orchestrated by the conserved ATG machinery, including the ULK1 initiation complex and the PI3K III/Beclin 1 nucleation complex. Macroautophagy is the dominant pathway induced by starvation, stress, and many pharmacological interventions and is the primary focus of most therapeutic autophagy modulation.

label: Microautophagy
description: Microautophagy involves the direct engulfment of cytoplasmic cargo by the lysosomal (or vacuolar) membrane through invagination, tubulation, or protrusion of the limiting membrane, without the requirement for a distinct autophagosome intermediate. The entrapped material is then internalized into the lysosomal lumen for degradation, a process that is particularly prominent in yeast vacuoles and in mammalian late endosomes/multivesicular bodies. Compared with macroautophagy, microautophagy operates with less selectivity and is regulated by distinct machineries, though it similarly contributes to organelle and protein turnover. It plays roles in lipid droplet turnover, membrane protein degradation, and quality control under both basal and stress conditions.

label: Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy
description: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) is a selective form of lysosomal degradation in which individual soluble cytosolic proteins bearing a pentapeptide KFERQ-like targeting motif are recognized by the cytosolic chaperone HSC70. The substrate-chaperone complex is then delivered to the lysosomal membrane, where the receptor LAMP-2A monomers translocate the unfolded substrate across the membrane into the lumen for degradation. Unlike macro- and microautophagy, CMA degrades one protein at a time and does not require membrane engulfment or autophagosome formation. CMA activity declines with age and is implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer, and it is subject to regulation by mTORC2 and other signaling nodes.

label: ULK1
description: ULK1 functions within a stable initiation complex containing ATG13, FIP200 (RB1CC1), and ATG101, which nucleates autophagosome formation in response to nutrient status. Directionally, the complex sits upstream of autophagy initiation. SIRT1 deacetylates and activates ULK1 within this complex, positioning sirtuins at the top of the autophagic machinery. The ULK1 complex integrates signals from AMPK and mTORC1, which either activate or inhibit it depending on energy and nutrient state. This makes the initiation complex the central decision point for whether autophagy proceeds.

label: PI3K III complex
description: The class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K III) complex, centered on Vps34 and including Beclin 1, Atg14, Vps15, and Ambra-1, generates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes to drive autophagosome nucleation. PI3P recruits effector proteins carrying PI3P-binding domains that organize the expanding phagophore and tether downstream ATG conjugation systems. Beclin 1 is a tumor suppressor whose activity is modulated by interacting partners and by anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins that restrain autophagy under fed conditions. This nucleation complex functions immediately downstream of the ULK1 initiator and is a critical control node for the magnitude of autophagic responses.

label: Intermittent Fasting
description: SIRT3 is induced by intermittent fasting, which enhances mitochondrial health and stress resistance, paralleling caloric restriction. Directionally, fasting sits upstream of SIRT3 induction. This raises the protective SIRT3/SIRT4 ratio and counters the age-related decline in mitochondrial function, and it is a translatable lifestyle intervention engaging sirtuin biology. By increasing SIRT3, intermittent fasting promotes oxidative metabolism, antioxidant defense, and mitochondrial quality control. These effects contribute to the metabolic benefits of fasting, including improved insulin sensitivity and resistance to age-related dysfunction.

label: Beclin 1
description: Beclin 1 is a core autophagy protein and a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor whose monoallelic deletion is frequently observed in human ovarian, breast, and prostate cancers. Loss of one BECN1 allele reduces autophagic flux, increasing susceptibility to oxidative damage, genomic instability, and inflammation that favor tumor initiation. Mechanistically, Beclin 1 functions as the scaffold of the PI3K III nucleation complex, and its interaction with Bcl-2 family members further couples autophagy to apoptotic regulation. Its frequent deletion in epithelial cancers established autophagy as a genuine tumor-suppression pathway.

label: Tumor suppressor
description: Bik acts as Tumor Suppressor. Bik is a BH3-only protein that directly activates Bax/Bak and is itself suppressed by oncogenic kinase signaling. A tumor suppressor is a gene or protein whose loss of function removes a constraint on proliferation or death, fostering cancer. The relationship is directional, with Bik acting as the operative agent upon Tumor Suppressor rather than the reverse. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

label: RAS
description: Activated RAS (e.g., HRASG12V) is a prototypical OIS-inducing oncogene, driving hyperproliferation and replication stress that triggers senescence as a tumor-suppressive failsafe. RAS signaling pushes cells into S-phase at excessive frequency, generating DNA damage that stabilizes p53 and derepresses p16, enforcing durable arrest. The relationship is a foundational model of OIS, first described by Serrano in 1997, and is extensively validated across cell and animal systems. It underlies the concept of oncogene-induced tumor-suppressive barriers.

label: Dietary Restriction
description: Dietary restriction (DR) and its variants are among the most potent physiological activators of autophagy, engaging the pathway in most cultured cells and across many organs in vivo. By lowering circulating nutrients and insulin while raising AMP/ATP ratios, DR relieves mTORC1 inhibition and activates AMPK, thereby de-repressing the ULK1 complex and TFEB-dependent lysosomal programs. In model organisms such as C. elegans, DR induces autophagy through coordinated transcriptional changes mediated by orthologs like HLH-30/TFEB. The health- and lifespan-extending effects of DR are widely attributed in substantial part to this induction of adaptive autophagy.

label: Caloric Restriction Mimetics
description: Caloric restriction mimetics are pharmacological agents that reproduce the metabolic and autophagic benefits of caloric restriction without sustained food reduction. Representatives such as 2-deoxyglucose, metformin, and spermidine activate AMPK and/or inhibit mTORC1, recapitulating the low-energy signaling state that drives autophagy. By mimicking nutrient scarcity at the signaling level, these compounds induce lysosomal and autophagic gene programs similar to those engaged during DR. They are attractive translationally because they avoid the practical and compliance limitations of long-term dietary restriction in humans.

label: Cisplatin
description: Cancer is treated by Cisplatin. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Cisplatin is a platinum compound that forms intra- and inter-strand DNA crosslinks, triggering damage responses that can culminate in senescence or death. The directionality runs from Cisplatin toward Cancer, so Cisplatin is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

label: Autophagic flux
description: Autophagic flux—the complete rate of cargo delivery to and degradation within lysosomes—declines progressively with age in many tissues. This decline stems from impaired initiation, reduced lysosomal proteolytic capacity, and accumulated lipofuscin that compromises lysosomal function, producing a state of proteostatic insufficiency. The resulting accumulation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates contributes centrally to the aging phenotype and to age-related diseases such as neurodegeneration and sarcopenia. Restoration of autophagic flux is therefore a major hypothesized mechanism through which longevity interventions exert their benefits.

label: Autophagy Inducer
description: Rapamycin is an autophagy inducer that activates ULK1 via mTOR inhibition, clearing damaged organelles and limiting inflammasome activation and mitochondrial DAMP release. This autophagic action contributes to its senomorphic and healthspan benefits, counteracting several senescence-associated defects in quality control. By restoring autophagic flux, it reduces the DAMPs that feed the SASP and inflammaging. The autophagy-inducing property is central to rapamycin's anti-aging profile and complements its direct suppression of SASP translation.

label: Immune Aging
description: Autophagy-inducing interventions have been shown to rejuvenate features of adaptive immune aging, a process characterized by thymic involution, reduced naïve T cell output, and diminished responses to vaccination and infection. By clearing damaged mitochondria and improving proteostasis in lymphocytes, autophagy inducers restore hematopoietic stem cell function and enhance memory CD8+ T cell generation. Pharmacological or dietary activation of autophagy counteracts the functional defects that accumulate in immune cells with age. These effects position autophagy enhancement as a plausible strategy to mitigate immunosenescence.

label: Spermidine
description: Spermidine induces autophagy without caloric deficit by directly inhibiting histone acetyltransferase p300, causing global deacetylation and upregulation of Atg gene transcription.

label: B Cell responses
source_file: _document_ - The autophagy enhancer spermidine reverses arterial aging.md
description: Spermidine supplementation rejuvenates age-impaired B cell responses by inducing autophagy in memory T and B lymphocytes, restoring their functional competence. The polyamine's ability to clear damaged organelles and enhance proteostasis in these cells counteracts the decline in vaccine responsiveness seen with immune aging. By supporting lymphoid cell fitness, spermidine addresses a key component of immunosenescence through an autophagy-dependent mechanism. These effects complement its broader rejuvenation of adaptive immunity.

label: eIF5A
description: Spermidine drives eIF5A hypusination, which promotes TFEB translation, leading to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis.

label: Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype
description: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) is the ensemble of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and matrix-remodeling enzymes secreted by senescent cells. Accumulation of senescent cells with age creates a chronic, low-grade inflammatory milieu that drives inflammaging—the sterile inflammation implicated in nearly all age-related diseases. SASP factors recruit immune cells, promote fibrosis, and induce paracrine senescence in neighboring cells, establishing feed-forward tissue deterioration. Targeting senescent cells or their SASP is a major therapeutic avenue to reduce inflammaging.

label: Th17 inflammatory profile
source_file: _document_ - Autophagy takes it all – autophagy inducers target immune aging.md
description: Metformin reverses the pro-inflammatory Th17 CD4+ T cell profile toward a more juvenile, balanced phenotype, an effect attributed to enhancement of autophagic flux within lymphocytes. By activating AMPK and inducing autophagy, metformin reduces the mitochondrial and metabolic perturbations that favor pathogenic Th17 differentiation. This phenotypic rebalancing may contribute to the drug's anti-inflammatory and immune-modulatory benefits beyond glycemic control. The observation links metformin's autophagy-inducing capacity to attenuation of age- and inflammation-associated T cell skewing.

label: MiT/TFE family
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: TFEB belongs to the MiT/TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper transcription factors, which also includes TFE3, MITF, and TFEC. Members of this family share conserved DNA-binding and dimerization domains and regulate overlapping sets of lysosomal and autophagic target genes. The family's defining feature is responsiveness to nutrient and stress signals that control nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling. TFEB and TFE3 are the principal mediators of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network.

label: CLEAR Element
description: TFEB binds to Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) elements—a conserved 10-base-pair motif (GTCACGTGAC) present in the promoters of numerous lysosomal and autophagy genes. Through this binding, TFEB drives the coordinated transcriptional upregulation of the entire autophagy-lysosomal network. CLEAR-mediated regulation allows cells to mount a unified response that expands degradative capacity in tandem with autophagic initiation. The CLEAR network is the molecular basis for TFEB's role as a master regulator of cellular clearance.

label: Autophagy-lysosomal pathway
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: TFEB is a master transcriptional regulator of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, coordinating the expression of genes required for autophagosome formation, cargo recognition, lysosomal biogenesis, and substrate degradation. Its activation simultaneously boosts both the supply of autophagosomes and the degradative capacity of lysosomes, ensuring coherent flux rather than unbalanced initiation. TFEB thereby couples the two halves of autophagy—sequestration and degradation—into a single coordinated program. Dysregulation of this axis contributes to lysosomal storage disorders, neurodegeneration, and cancer.

label: 14-3-3 protein
description: Once TFEB is phosphorylated at serine 211 by mTORC1, 14-3-3 proteins bind the phosphorylated motif and mask the transcription factor's nuclear localization signal. This cytosolic sequestration prevents TFEB from accessing CLEAR elements in the nucleus, thereby suppressing expression of lysosomal and autophagic genes. The 14-3-3 interaction thereby converts a single phosphorylation event into a durable spatial exclusion of TFEB. Disruption of this complex is a key step in starvation- and drug-induced TFEB activation.

label: TFEB in cytosol
description: Once TFEB is phosphorylated at serine 211 by mTORC1, 14-3-3 proteins bind the phosphorylated motif and mask the transcription factor's nuclear localization signal. This cytosolic sequestration prevents TFEB from accessing CLEAR elements in the nucleus, thereby suppressing expression of lysosomal and autophagic genes. The 14-3-3 interaction thereby converts a single phosphorylation event into a durable spatial exclusion of TFEB. Disruption of this complex is a key step in starvation- and drug-induced TFEB activation.

label: TRPML1
description: TRPML1 (mucolipin-1) is a lysosomal cation channel that releases Ca2+ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol in response to stimuli such as PI(3,5)P2 or lumenal cues. The resulting local calcium signal activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and promotes its nuclear translocation. Through this mechanism, TRPML1 functionally links lysosomal ion homeostasis to the transcriptional activation of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Loss of TRPML1 underlies the lysosomal storage disorder mucolipidosis type IV.

label: Ca2+ from lysosomes
description: TRPML1 (mucolipin-1) is a lysosomal cation channel that releases Ca2+ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol in response to stimuli such as PI(3,5)P2 or lumenal cues. The resulting local calcium signal activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and promotes its nuclear translocation. Through this mechanism, TRPML1 functionally links lysosomal ion homeostasis to the transcriptional activation of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Loss of TRPML1 underlies the lysosomal storage disorder mucolipidosis type IV.

label: TFEB at S466/S467/S469
description: AMPK phosphorylates TFEB on a cluster of serine residues (S466, S467, S469) located in its C-terminal regulatory region in response to energy stress. These phosphorylations enhance TFEB transcriptional activity and promote its nuclear accumulation, synergizing with the relief of mTORC1 repression. The modification thereby directly couples low cellular energy status to activation of the autophagy-lysosomal transcriptional program. This AMPK-TFEB axis provides a transcription-level reinforcement of the rapid post-translational induction of autophagy.

label: TFEB at S134/S138
description: Glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β) phosphorylates TFEB at serines 134 and 138, residues that influence its subcellular localization and association with lysosomal membranes. These phosphorylations contribute to the regulated shuttling of TFEB and modulate its activity in response to Wnt and growth-factor signaling contexts. Because GSK3β activity is itself controlled by Akt and by nutrient state, this modification embeds TFEB within the broader insulin/PI3K signaling network. The sites complement the better-characterized S211 mark in fine-tuning TFEB localization.

label: CDK4/6
description: Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6), central drivers of G1 cell-cycle progression, phosphorylate TFEB at serine 142 and promote its nuclear export through a CRM1-dependent mechanism. This action sequesters TFEB in the cytoplasm during phases of active proliferation, when degradative programs are downregulated. Conversely, pharmacological CDK4/6 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear retention and enhances lysosome biogenesis and autophagy. The CDK4/6-TFEB link couples cell-cycle state to the metabolic and degradative status of the cell.

label: MAP4K3
description: MAP4K3 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 3, an N-terminal modification that primes TFEB for subsequent phosphorylation at S211 by mTORC1. This hierarchical phosphorylation reveals that TFEB regulation involves ordered, multi-site modification in which upstream kinases license downstream ones. By enabling the mTORC1 repressive mark, MAP4K3 integrates amino-acid and growth-factor inputs into TFEB control. The finding adds a further layer of complexity to the kinase network governing lysosomal gene transcription.

label: TFEB at S3
description: MAP4K3 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 3, an N-terminal modification that primes TFEB for subsequent phosphorylation at S211 by mTORC1. This hierarchical phosphorylation reveals that TFEB regulation involves ordered, multi-site modification in which upstream kinases license downstream ones. By enabling the mTORC1 repressive mark, MAP4K3 integrates amino-acid and growth-factor inputs into TFEB control. The finding adds a further layer of complexity to the kinase network governing lysosomal gene transcription.

label: TFEB at S401
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: In contrast to its S211 effect, p38 MAPK phosphorylates TFEB at serine 401 in a manner that promotes nuclear translocation in specific cell types such as monocytes. This site-specific divergence illustrates that p38 can either retain or activate TFEB depending on cell context and the constellation of concurrent modifications. Such opposing outcomes highlight the combinatorial code by which multiple phosphorylations determine TFEB localization. The monocyte-specific response implicates TFEB in immune cell activation and inflammatory programs.

label: TFEB at K274/K279
description: GCN5, a lysine acetyltransferase, acetylates TFEB at lysines 274 and 279 within its DNA-binding domain, an modification that hinders TFEB dimerization and its ability to bind CLEAR elements. Acetylation at these sites therefore represses TFEB transcriptional activity independently of its localization. This post-translational modification expands the regulatory vocabulary of TFEB beyond phosphorylation to include acetylation-dependent control of DNA engagement. The finding situates TFEB within the broader acetylome that governs transcription factor function.

label: Phosphorylated TFEB
description: STUB1 (CHIP), an E3 ubiquitin ligase, recognizes and ubiquitinates phosphorylated TFEB, targeting the transcription factor for proteasomal degradation. This mechanism ensures that TFEB levels are coupled to its phosphorylation state, providing a negative-feedback brake on sustained activation. By eliminating phosphorylated, cytosolically retained TFEB, STUB1 limits the accumulation of inactive protein and fine-tunes the amplitude of the autophagic response. The pathway connects TFEB turnover to the ubiquitin-proteasome system rather than to lysosomal degradation.

label: TNKS1
description: Tankyrase 1 (TNKS1) poly-ADP-ribosylates (PARsylates) TFEB, a modification that promotes its nuclear translocation and activation of target genes. PARsylation addsADP-ribose polymers that alter TFEB interactions and trafficking, providing a non-phosphorylation route to TFEB activation. This modification broadens the enzymatic toolkit—alongside kinases, phosphatases, acetylases, and ubiquitin ligases—that regulates the autophagy-lysosomal master switch. The TNKS1-TFEB relationship suggests potential crosstalk with Wnt/β-catenin and other PARsylation-dependent pathways.

label: K316
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: TFEB undergoes SUMOylation at lysine 316, a small ubiquitin-like modifier conjugation that attenuates its transcriptional activity. SUMOylation typically modulates protein-protein interactions and subnuclear compartmentalization, and at K316 it dampens TFEB-driven expression of lysosomal genes. This modification adds another layer to the post-translational code governing TFEB, acting in opposition to activatory marks such as deacetylation. The reversibility of SUMOylation by SENPs allows dynamic tuning of the degradative program.

label: Oxidation at C212
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: Oxidation of TFEB at cysteine 212—for example by reactive oxygen species or oxidants—impairs mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation at adjacent regulatory sites and thereby enhances TFEB activity. This redox-sensitive control links cellular oxidative status directly to activation of the lysosomal-autophagy program, functioning as a stress sensor. By relieving kinase repression under oxidative conditions, TFEB oxidation promotes clearance of damaged components that generate ROS. The C212 modification exemplifies how cysteine-based redox switches integrate stress signaling with degradative transcription.

label: S-sulfhydration at C212
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: S-sulfhydration of TFEB at cysteine 212, catalyzed by the cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH)-derived hydrogen sulfide (H2S) system, promotes its nuclear translocation and activation. This post-translational modification, distinct from oxidation, converts C212 into a persulfide that alters TFEB interactions and favors a transcriptionally active state. The regulation ties sulfur metabolism and H2S signaling to the autophagy-lysosomal network, with implications for cardiovascular and neurodegenerative protection. It represents a gasotransmitter-based mechanism controlling cellular clearance.

label: MYC
description: The SIRT7-Myc axis is bidirectional: SIRT7 assembles with Myc at ribosomal protein (RP) gene promoters to silence gene expression and relieve ER stress, while Myc-driven proliferation opposes SIRT7-dependent growth-quiescence programs in some contexts; Table 3 lists Myc among negative regulators of SIRT7 (Shin et al., 2013, PMID 24210820).

label: TFEB for CLEAR element
description: The oncogenic transcription factor MYC competes with TFEB for binding to CLEAR elements in the promoters of lysosomal and autophagy genes. By occupying these sites, MYC represses the TFEB-driven transcriptional program while simultaneously driving its own proliferative gene network. This competitive binding creates a molecular antagonism between growth-promoting and degradative transcriptional programs. The interplay explains how MYC-high tumors suppress autophagy-lysosomal capacity even as they increase metabolic demand.

label: METTL3
description: METTL3 is the catalytic subunit of the methyltransferase complex that deposits N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant internal modification of messenger RNA in mammalian cells. Together with the adaptor protein METTL14, METTL3 methylates the N6 position of adenosine in mRNA, and the resulting m6A mark regulates RNA stability, splicing, translation, and export. Beyond its RNA-methylation role, the METTL3-METTL14 complex also facilitates senescence-associated enhancer-promoter contacts and SASP expression in oncogene-induced senescence.

label: TFEB expression
description: METTL3, the catalytic subunit of the m6A methyltransferase complex, methylates TFEB mRNA at N6-methyladenosine residues, a mark that targets the transcript for destabilization and degradation. By reducing TFEB mRNA stability, METTL3 negatively regulates TFEB protein abundance and consequently the autophagy-lysosomal program. This epitranscriptomic control links RNA methylation to degradative pathway output. The finding situates TFEB within the expanding regulatory influence of m6A modification on stress-response genes.

label: PDCD4
description: Programmed cell death protein 4 (PDCD4) suppresses TFEB translation by binding eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A) and inhibiting the RNA helicase activity required for ribosome scanning of the TFEB mRNA. This translational blockade limits TFEB protein synthesis independently of its transcriptional or degradative regulation. PDCD4 thereby acts as a brake on the autophagy-lysosomal program at the level of protein synthesis. Its own downregulation in cancer may contribute to the elevated TFEB activity observed in some malignancies.

label: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
description: In Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) syndrome, caused by Folliculin (FLCN) mutations, TFEB becomes hyperactivated and drives a renal cystic and tumor-prone phenotype. Loss of FLCN dysregulates mTOR and related signaling such that TFEB-mediated lysosomal and proliferative programs are inappropriately engaged in renal epithelial cells. This pathogenic role contrasts with TFEB's generally protective function in neurodegeneration and aging. The BHD example demonstrates that excessive or context-inappropriate TFEB activation can be deleterious.

label: Glutamine metabolism
description: SIRT4 inhibits glutamine metabolism in colorectal cancer cells—for example by restraining GDH-dependent anaplerosis—acting as a tumor suppressor that limits nutrient fueling of proliferation. Directionally, SIRT4 sits upstream of suppressed glutamine catabolism. This constrains the glutamine addiction of many tumors, which rely on glutamine as a carbon and nitrogen source. It illustrates SIRT4's context-dependent tumor-suppressive role, contrasting with its metabolic-brake functions in normal tissue. Because glutamine metabolism supports both bioenergetics and nucleotide synthesis in cancer, SIRT4-mediated suppression of anaplerosis represents a potential therapeutic strategy.

label: Eltrombopag
description: Eltrombopag (EO), a small-molecule thrombopoietin receptor agonist, was identified as the first direct inhibitor of TFEB, disrupting TFEB-DNA interactions at CLEAR elements. By preventing TFEB from binding its target promoters, EO blocks transcriptional activation of the autophagy-lysosomal network. This tool compound has enabled dissection of TFEB-dependent versus independent autophagy and has therapeutic implications where TFEB hyperactivation is pathogenic. Its discovery established pharmacological feasibility of directly targeting the MiT/TFE family.

label: TFEB at S122
description: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 122, an additional N-terminal regulatory site that contributes to cytoplasmic retention of the transcription factor under nutrient-rich conditions. Alongside S142 and S211, S122 forms part of the multi-site phosphorylation code through which mTORC1 enforces TFEB exclusion from the nucleus. Dephosphorylation of these sites by phosphatases such as PP2A is required for nuclear translocation. The multiplicity of mTORC1 sites provides tunable, robust control of lysosomal gene transcription.

label: TFEB at S138
description: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 138, a residue also modified by GSK3β, and this phosphorylation promotes nuclear export of TFEB, complementing the cytosolic retention imposed at other sites. The accumulation of phosphates across the N-terminal regulatory region collectively suppresses TFEB transcriptional activity. Relief of S138 phosphorylation facilitates nuclear accumulation and activation of the autophagy-lysosomal program. This site therefore participates in the coordinated mTORC1 restraint of cellular clearance.

label: TFEB at S122/S109/S114
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) dephosphorylates TFEB at serines 122, 109, and 114, removing repressive mTORC1 and other kinase marks to permit TFEB nuclear translocation. By counteracting the multiple N-terminal phosphorylations that enforce cytosolic retention, PP2A acts as a key permissive switch for TFEB activation. Its activity is regulated by nutrient state and by regulatory subunits that target it to TFEB. Through this dephosphorylation, PP2A enables the rapid engagement of lysosomal biogenesis when mTORC1 is inhibited.

label: TFEB at S467
description: Akt phosphorylates TFEB at serine 467, a C-terminal residue within the regulatory cluster that contributes to cytoplasmic retention of the transcription factor downstream of insulin and growth-factor signaling. By adding to the phosphorylation state of TFEB, Akt reinforces the anabolic, autophagy-suppressed state promoted by PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling. This modification complements mTORC1-mediated marks and integrates proliferative cues with repression of degradative transcription. The Akt-TFEB link embeds TFEB within the canonical survival signaling network.

label: TFEB at S461/S462/S466/S468
description: Protein kinase C beta (PKCβ) phosphorylates TFEB at a cluster of C-terminal serines (461, 462, 466, 468), modifications that promote TFEB stability rather than suppressing it. Enhanced stability increases the available pool of TFEB that can be activated when nuclear entry is permitted. This contrasts with the predominantly inhibitory phosphorylations at N-terminal mTORC1 sites, illustrating that C-terminal modifications can be activatory. The PKCβ-TFEB relationship adds nuance to the site-specific regulatory code governing the transcription factor.

label: TFEB at K91/K103/K116/K430
description: Acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1 (ACAT1) acetylates TFEB at multiple lysines (K91, K103, K116, K430), an enzymatic activity that, in this context, promotes TFEB nuclear translocation and DNA binding. These acetylations counteract repressive deacetylation cycles and enhance TFEB's ability to engage CLEAR elements, thereby boosting autophagy-lysosomal transcription. The observation that ACAT1-mediated acetylation can be activatory contrasts with the repressive acetylation by GCN5 at other sites. The net effect depends on the specific lysine and cellular context, underscoring the complexity of TFEB acetylation.

label: Lysosome
description: The lysosome is the cell's terminal degradation center, containing acidic hydrolases that break down proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy. Beyond catabolism, lysosomes serve as signaling hubs that integrate nutrient and growth-factor inputs, most notably by hosting the activation of mTORC1 at their surface. This duality—as both waste-disposal organelle and metabolic command post—places lysosomes at the center of cellular homeostasis, development, and aging. Lysosomal dysfunction underlies a broad spectrum of storage and degenerative diseases.

label: Degradation center and signaling hub
description: The lysosome is the cell's terminal degradation center, containing acidic hydrolases that break down proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy. Beyond catabolism, lysosomes serve as signaling hubs that integrate nutrient and growth-factor inputs, most notably by hosting the activation of mTORC1 at their surface. This duality—as both waste-disposal organelle and metabolic command post—places lysosomes at the center of cellular homeostasis, development, and aging. Lysosomal dysfunction underlies a broad spectrum of storage and degenerative diseases.

label: Lysosome biogenesis
source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
description: TFEB activates lysosome biogenesis by binding CLEAR elements in the promoters of genes encoding lysosomal membrane proteins, hydrolases, and v-ATPase subunits, coordinately increasing lysosomal number and capacity. This transcriptional program ensures that autophagic demand is matched by degradative capacity, preventing futile autophagosome accumulation. TFEB activation therefore expands the entire lysosomal network rather than individual enzymes. The effect is a cornerstone of cellular adaptation to starvation and stress.

label: TFE3
description: TFE3, the closely related MiT/TFE family member, also binds CLEAR elements and induces lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in response to nutrient deprivation and stress. Like TFEB, TFE3 is repressed by mTORC1 through phosphorylation and released upon starvation, calcineurin activation, or ER stress. The overlapping but non-identical target sets of TFEB and TFE3 provide redundancy and specificity in the lysosomal program. TFE3's distinct regulation, including PERK-dependent activation, broadens the stress-responsive control of degradation.

label: Lysosomal surface
description: mTORC1 is recruited to the lysosomal surface, where it encounters its activator Rheb and receives upstream amino-acid and growth-factor inputs necessary for full activation. This spatial recruitment, mediated by Rag GTPases and the Ragulator scaffold, converts the lysosome into the signaling platform for mTORC1. Only when docked at the lysosome can mTORC1 efficiently phosphorylate its substrates, including TFEB and ULK1. Thus lysosomal localization is essential for mTORC1 function and for its inhibition of autophagy.

label: Ragulator
description: The Ragulator is a multiprotein scaffold anchored at the lysosomal membrane that interacts with Rag GTPases to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface in response to amino acids. By tethering the Rag-mTORC1 complex at the lysosome, Ragulator enables amino-acid sensing to converge with Rheb-mediated activation. Loss of Ragulator disrupts nutrient-dependent mTORC1 signaling and de-represses autophagy. The complex is therefore the lynchpin coupling lysosomal amino-acid detection to mTORC1 and autophagy control.

label: mTORC1 to lysosomes
description: The Ragulator is a multiprotein scaffold anchored at the lysosomal membrane that interacts with Rag GTPases to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface in response to amino acids. By tethering the Rag-mTORC1 complex at the lysosome, Ragulator enables amino-acid sensing to converge with Rheb-mediated activation. Loss of Ragulator disrupts nutrient-dependent mTORC1 signaling and de-represses autophagy. The complex is therefore the lynchpin coupling lysosomal amino-acid detection to mTORC1 and autophagy control.

label: PIKfyve
description: PIKfyve is a phosphoinositide kinase that converts phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) into phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P2) on endolysosomal membranes. PI(3,5)P2 serves as a crucial lipid messenger that regulates membrane trafficking, vacuole homeostasis, and the activity of the lysosomal channel TRPML1. By generating PI(3,5)P2, PIKfyve controls lysosomal morphology and the calcium release that activates calcineurin-TFEB signaling. Its inhibition causes massive lysosomal vacuolation, underscoring its centrality to lysosomal function.

label: PtdIns(3,5)P2
description: PIKfyve is a phosphoinositide kinase that converts phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) into phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P2) on endolysosomal membranes. PI(3,5)P2 serves as a crucial lipid messenger that regulates membrane trafficking, vacuole homeostasis, and the activity of the lysosomal channel TRPML1. By generating PI(3,5)P2, PIKfyve controls lysosomal morphology and the calcium release that activates calcineurin-TFEB signaling. Its inhibition causes massive lysosomal vacuolation, underscoring its centrality to lysosomal function.

label: Lysosomal Ca2+ efflux
description: TRPML1 is the principal lysosomal Ca2+ release channel, activated by PI(3,5)P2 and other cues to efflux Ca2+ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. The released Ca2+ activates calcineurin, driving TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and thereby coupling ion flux to transcriptional activation of lysosomal biogenesis. TRPML1 also participates in lysosomal trafficking and autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Loss of TRPML1 causes mucolipidosis type IV, a lysosomal storage disorder, confirming its essential role in degradative homeostasis.

label: Autophagic Lysosome Reformation
description: Autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR) is the process by which spent autolysosomes tubulate and bud off new lysosomes to restore the lysosomal pool after autophagy. ALR requires the coordinated actions of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), clathrin, and adaptor proteins AP2 and AP4 to drive membrane scission and vesicle formation. This reformation step is essential to prevent lysosomal depletion during sustained autophagy. Defects in ALR cause accumulation of enlarged autolysosomes and impaired degradative capacity.

label: PtdIns(4,5)P2
description: Autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR) is the process by which spent autolysosomes tubulate and bud off new lysosomes to restore the lysosomal pool after autophagy. ALR requires the coordinated actions of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), clathrin, and adaptor proteins AP2 and AP4 to drive membrane scission and vesicle formation. This reformation step is essential to prevent lysosomal depletion during sustained autophagy. Defects in ALR cause accumulation of enlarged autolysosomes and impaired degradative capacity.

label: ZKSCAN3
description: ZKSCAN3 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that represses the expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes, acting in opposition to TFEB/TFE3. Under basal conditions it limits autophagic and lysosomal capacity, and its inhibition or loss enhances cellular clearance. ZKSCAN3 thereby functions as a transcriptional brake on the degradative network, complementary to the post-translational repression by mTORC1. Targeting ZKSCAN3 has been proposed as a strategy to boost autophagy in disease.

label: Lysosomal and autophagy genes
description: ZKSCAN3 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that represses the expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes, acting in opposition to TFEB/TFE3. Under basal conditions it limits autophagic and lysosomal capacity, and its inhibition or loss enhances cellular clearance. ZKSCAN3 thereby functions as a transcriptional brake on the degradative network, complementary to the post-translational repression by mTORC1. Targeting ZKSCAN3 has been proposed as a strategy to boost autophagy in disease.

label: TFEB at Ser142/Ser211
description: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at both serine 142 and serine 211, two residues whose combined modification enforces 14-3-3 binding and robust cytosolic retention of the transcription factor. These sites act synergistically to prevent TFEB nuclear entry and thus block activation of the autophagy-lysosomal program under nutrient-replete conditions. Dephosphorylation of both marks is required for full TFEB activation during starvation. The dual-site control exemplifies the redundancy mTORC1 employs to firmly suppress degradative transcription.

label: TFEB independent of mTOR
description: Protein kinase C (PKC) activation induces TFEB nuclear translocation through an mTORC1-independent route, primarily by inactivating GSK3β, which otherwise phosphorylates TFEB at cytosolic-retention sites. This alternative regulatory input allows TFEB to be engaged by diacylglycerol and calcium signaling without requiring nutrient deprivation. The pathway diversifies the contexts—such as immune cell activation—in which the autophagy-lysosomal program can be turned on. It demonstrates that TFEB is controlled by parallel kinase networks rather than solely by mTOR.

label: TFEB at Ser142
description: CDK4/6 phosphorylate TFEB at serine 142, driving CRM1-dependent nuclear export and cytoplasmic sequestration during cell-cycle progression. This modification aligns TFEB repression with the biosynthetic demands of dividing cells, when autophagy is downregulated. Pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibitors relieve this constraint, permitting TFEB nuclear accumulation and enhancing lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux. The axis thereby couples cell-cycle machinery to the metabolic state of the cell.

label: SLC-36.1
description: SLC-36.1 (a solute carrier) forms a complex with the PPK-3/PIKfyve kinase module to regulate phagocytic lysosome reformation (PLR), the process by which phagolysosomes regenerate new lysosomes after phagocytosis. By influencing PI(3,5)P2 generation and membrane dynamics, this complex ensures restoration of the lysosomal pool following immune or clearance challenges. Defects in PLR impair the ability of phagocytes to sustain repeated rounds of degradation. The pathway connects solute transport and phosphoinositide metabolism to innate immune function.

label: Phagocytic Lysosome Reformation
description: SLC-36.1 (a solute carrier) forms a complex with the PPK-3/PIKfyve kinase module to regulate phagocytic lysosome reformation (PLR), the process by which phagolysosomes regenerate new lysosomes after phagocytosis. By influencing PI(3,5)P2 generation and membrane dynamics, this complex ensures restoration of the lysosomal pool following immune or clearance challenges. Defects in PLR impair the ability of phagocytes to sustain repeated rounds of degradation. The pathway connects solute transport and phosphoinositide metabolism to innate immune function.

label: Intracellular and extracellular signals
description: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway integrates a wide array of intracellular and extracellular cues—including growth factors, insulin, amino acids, oxygen, and energy status—to coordinate cell growth, metabolism, proliferation, and survival. Through its two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, it translates these inputs into decisions about biosynthesis versus catabolism, notably by inhibiting autophagy when resources are abundant. This central integrator role makes mTOR a nodal control point for physiology and a target for cancer, aging, and metabolic disease. Its dysregulation is implicated in nearly every major chronic disease.

label: mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, Deptor
description: mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) is composed of five core subunits: the catalytic kinase mTOR, the scaffold Raptor (which binds substrates and Rag GTPases), mLST8 (stabilizing the kinase domain), the inhibitory subunit PRAS40, and the negative regulator Deptor. This stoichiometric assembly defines mTORC1's substrate specificity and its sensitivity to upstream inputs such as amino acids and insulin. Raptor is essential for recruitment of mTORC1 to lysosomes and for phosphorylation of canonical substrates like S6K1 and 4E-BP1. The composition distinguishes mTORC1 from mTORC2, which shares mTOR, mLST8, and Deptor but includes Rictor instead of Raptor.

label: mTOR, Rictor, mSIN1, Protor-1, mLST8, Deptor
description: mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) comprises six core proteins: mTOR, Rictor (its defining scaffold), mSIN1 (required for mTORC2 integrity and Akt phosphorylation), Protor-1, mLST8, and the negative regulator Deptor. mTORC2 is best known for phosphorylating and activating Akt at Ser473 and for regulating cytoskeletal organization and cell survival. Unlike mTORC1, mTORC2 is not acutely rapamycin-sensitive and is not directly recruited to lysosomes by Rag GTPases. Its distinct composition underlies its separate physiological roles in metabolism and actin dynamics.

label: Protein synthesis
description: mTORC1 promotes cap-dependent protein synthesis by phosphorylating the eukaryotic initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), releasing eIF4E to initiate translation, and by phosphorylating S6 kinase 1 (S6K1), which enhances ribosome biogenesis and translational capacity. These outputs prioritize anabolic processes when nutrients and growth factors are plentiful. The stimulation of protein synthesis is a major consumer of cellular energy and amino acids, balanced against the catabolic program of autophagy. Dysregulated mTORC1-driven translation contributes to hypertrophy and malignancy.

label: Lipid synthesis
description: mTORC1 promotes lipid and cholesterol synthesis by activating the sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBP1) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), transcription factors that drive expression of lipogenic and adipogenic enzymes. This anabolic output supports membrane biogenesis and energy storage during growth. The lipid-synthetic program is coordinated with mTORC1's stimulation of protein and nucleotide synthesis to build cellular mass. Its dysregulation contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome.

label: TSC1/TSC2
description: The TSC1-TSC2 tumor-suppressor complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the small G protein Rheb, converting active GTP-bound Rheb to its inactive GDP-bound form. Because only GTP-Rheb directly activates mTORC1, TSC1/TSC2 functions as a critical upstream brake on mTORC1 in response to energy, oxygen, and growth-factor signals. Loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 cause tuberous sclerosis complex, characterized by constitutive mTORC1 activation, hamartoma formation, and autophagy suppression. The complex is therefore a major gatekeeper of mTORC1 and cellular growth.

label: Rheb
description: Rheb (Ras homolog enriched in brain) is a small GTPase that directly binds and activates mTORC1 when in its GTP-bound state, provided mTORC1 is localized at the lysosomal surface. Rheb's activity is held in check by the TSC1/TSC2 GAP complex, making it the immediate effector that relays growth and nutrient signals to mTORC1. GTP-Rheb relieves the autoinhibitory conformation of mTORC1, enabling substrate phosphorylation. As the proximal activator, Rheb sits at the convergence point of multiple upstream inhibitory pathways.

label: Rag proteins
description: Rag GTPases (RagA/B and RagC/D) function as heterodimers that bind the mTORC1 subunit Raptor and promote relocalization of mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface, where activator Rheb resides. Amino-acid sufficiency favors the active Rag conformation, positioning mTORC1 for activation; amino-acid starvation inactivates Rags and disperses mTORC1, de-repressing autophagy. The Rags therefore act as amino-acid sensors that bridge nutrient availability to mTORC1 spatial activation. Their regulation by the Ragulator and GAPs (e.g., GATOR complexes) is central to nutrient signaling.

label: REDD1
description: REDD1 (regulated in development and DNA damage responses 1) inhibits mTORC1 specifically under hypoxia by binding and releasing TSC2 from inhibitory 14-3-3 association, thereby activating the TSC GAP complex. This allows Rheb to be converted to its inactive GDP form and mTORC1 to be suppressed, conserving energy when oxygen is limiting. REDD1 thus provides a hypoxia-responsive brake that engages autophagy and limits anabolic consumption. Its induction is transcriptionally controlled by HIF-1α, integrating oxygen sensing with mTORC1 regulation.

label: mTORC1 under hypoxia
description: REDD1 (regulated in development and DNA damage responses 1) inhibits mTORC1 specifically under hypoxia by binding and releasing TSC2 from inhibitory 14-3-3 association, thereby activating the TSC GAP complex. This allows Rheb to be converted to its inactive GDP form and mTORC1 to be suppressed, conserving energy when oxygen is limiting. REDD1 thus provides a hypoxia-responsive brake that engages autophagy and limits anabolic consumption. Its induction is transcriptionally controlled by HIF-1α, integrating oxygen sensing with mTORC1 regulation.

label: Akt at Ser473
description: mTORC2 phosphorylates Akt at serine 473 within its hydrophobic motif, a modification required for full Akt catalytic activation alongside PDK1-mediated phosphorylation at Thr308. Active Akt then drives survival, growth, and mTORC1 activation, establishing an mTORC2-to-Akt-to-mTORC1 signaling cascade. This relationship makes mTORC2 an upstream regulator of the same anabolic and autophagy-suppressing programs executed by mTORC1. mTORC2's role in Akt activation is central to its pro-survival and metabolic functions.

label: Cytoskeletal organization
description: mTORC2 regulates actin cytoskeleton organization and cell migration through phosphorylation of PKCα and via effects on paxillin, RhoA, and Rac1 signaling. These outputs control cell polarity, stress-fiber formation, and the ability of cells to remodel their architecture during growth and movement. Unlike mTORC1, mTORC2's roles are more closely tied to spatial organization and survival than to bulk nutrient sensing. Dysregulation of mTORC2-dependent cytoskeletal control contributes to cancer cell invasion and metastasis.

label: PRAS40
description: PRAS40 is an mTORC1-associated protein that acts as a negative regulator by competing for substrate binding and limiting mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly when the complex is in a low-activity state. Growth-factor signaling through Akt phosphorylates PRAS40, releasing its inhibition and permitting mTORC1 activation. Thus PRAS40 provides a built-in brake that is relieved by anabolic signals. Its dynamic association fine-tunes mTORC1 output in response to the cellular environment.

label: Deptor
description: Deptor is an endogenous inhibitor that binds both mTORC1 and mTORC2, suppressing the catalytic activity of each complex. By dampening both arms of mTOR signaling, Deptor broadly restrains anabolic growth, survival, and autophagy suppression. Its expression is itself feedback-regulated by mTORC1/mTORC2 activity, forming part of a homeostatic loop. Reduced Deptor levels in certain cancers correlate with hyperactive mTOR signaling, highlighting its tumor-suppressive potential.

label: mTORC1 and mTORC2
description: Deptor is an endogenous inhibitor that binds both mTORC1 and mTORC2, suppressing the catalytic activity of each complex. By dampening both arms of mTOR signaling, Deptor broadly restrains anabolic growth, survival, and autophagy suppression. Its expression is itself feedback-regulated by mTORC1/mTORC2 activity, forming part of a homeostatic loop. Reduced Deptor levels in certain cancers correlate with hyperactive mTOR signaling, highlighting its tumor-suppressive potential.

label: MXL-3
description: In C. elegans, the MAX-like transcription factor MXL-3 represses transcription of lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) when food is abundant, limiting lipid mobilization. This repression maintains lipid storage under fed conditions and is relieved during fasting, allowing lipolysis. MXL-3 thus acts as a nutritional gatekeeper of lysosomal lipid catabolism, analogous to MYC's repression of lysosomal programs in mammals. Its activity positions lipid degradation within the broader nutrient-responsive regulatory network.

label: Lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1,2,3,5)
description: In C. elegans, the MAX-like transcription factor MXL-3 represses transcription of lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) when food is abundant, limiting lipid mobilization. This repression maintains lipid storage under fed conditions and is relieved during fasting, allowing lipolysis. MXL-3 thus acts as a nutritional gatekeeper of lysosomal lipid catabolism, analogous to MYC's repression of lysosomal programs in mammals. Its activity positions lipid degradation within the broader nutrient-responsive regulatory network.

label: HLH-30
description: HLH-30, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian TFEB, induces expression of the lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) in response to fasting, promoting mobilization of stored lipids. This transcriptional activation mirrors TFEB's induction of lipolytic and autophagic programs in mammals during nutrient scarcity. The HLH-30–lipase axis provides a molecular explanation for fasting-induced lipophagy and lifespan extension in worms. It demonstrates deep conservation of the MiT/TFE nutrient-response program.

label: Lysosomal lipase genes
description: HLH-30, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian TFEB, induces expression of the lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) in response to fasting, promoting mobilization of stored lipids. This transcriptional activation mirrors TFEB's induction of lipolytic and autophagic programs in mammals during nutrient scarcity. The HLH-30–lipase axis provides a molecular explanation for fasting-induced lipophagy and lifespan extension in worms. It demonstrates deep conservation of the MiT/TFE nutrient-response program.

label: Intestinal nuclei during fasting
description: During fasting, MXL-3::GFP signal disappears from intestinal nuclei within about two hours, indicating that the repressor exits the nucleus and ceases to suppress its target genes. This delocalization is a rapid, nutrient-responsive event that permits de-repression of lysosomal lipase and autophagy genes. The nuclear export of MXL-3 complements the concurrent nuclear accumulation of HLH-30, creating a switch from storage to mobilization. The observation provides direct in vivo evidence for dynamic regulation of the lipid-degradation program.

label: Nucleus during fasting
description: HLH-30 translocates to and accumulates in intestinal nuclei of fasted C. elegans, where it activates the lysosomal, autophagic, and lipolytic transcriptional programs. This nuclear enrichment mirrors the starvation-induced nuclear entry of mammalian TFEB/TFE3 and is essential for the organism's adaptive response to food deprivation. The translocation is opposed by insulin/IGF and CeTOR signaling that retain HLH-30 cytoplasmically when food is available. Its nuclear localization thus serves as a key determinant of fasting-induced longevity.

label: LIPL-1
description: LIPL-1 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2, confirming its residence within the lysosomal lumen where it hydrolyzes stored triglycerides. Its expression is induced by HLH-30 during fasting, supporting lipophagy-mediated lipid mobilization. LIPL-1 is part of a family of lysosomal lipases (lipl-1 through lipl-5) that together govern organismal lipid turnover. Loss or reduction of these lipases impairs the ability to survive nutrient scarcity.

label: LipA
description: LIPL-1 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2, confirming its residence within the lysosomal lumen where it hydrolyzes stored triglycerides. Its expression is induced by HLH-30 during fasting, supporting lipophagy-mediated lipid mobilization. LIPL-1 is part of a family of lysosomal lipases (lipl-1 through lipl-5) that together govern organismal lipid turnover. Loss or reduction of these lipases impairs the ability to survive nutrient scarcity.

label: LIPL-3
description: LIPL-3 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that, like LIPL-1, co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2 and contributes to intralysosomal lipid hydrolysis. It is transcriptionally induced by HLH-30 under fasting conditions, enabling the breakdown of lipid droplets delivered via lipophagy. Together with other lipl family members, LIPL-3 is required for efficient energy mobilization during starvation. Its lysosomal localization anchors it within the autophagy-lysosomal degradative system.

label: MAX
description: The mammalian transcription factor MAX, a partner of MYC, is the functional homolog of C. elegans MXL-3, as expression of mouse MAX in worms rescued the mxl-3 mutant phenotype. This conservation indicates that the MYC/MAX network's repression of lysosomal and metabolic genes is an ancient feature retained from nematodes to mammals. The rescue experiment directly demonstrates mechanistic equivalence between the worm repressor and its mammalian counterpart. It strengthens the translational relevance of MXL-3 studies to human lipid and lysosomal regulation.

label: Lipophagy
description: Lipophagy—the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets—is conserved across metazoans, as shown by the fact that inactivation of the autophagy genes lgg-1 and lgg-2 in C. elegans leads to increased fat accumulation. By delivering lipid droplets to lysosomes for lipase-mediated hydrolysis, lipophagy mobilizes stored energy during fasting. The conservation from worms to mammals indicates an ancient and essential role for autophagy in lipid homeostasis. Defective lipophagy contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic disease in higher organisms.

label: Metazoans
description: Lipophagy—the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets—is conserved across metazoans, as shown by the fact that inactivation of the autophagy genes lgg-1 and lgg-2 in C. elegans leads to increased fat accumulation. By delivering lipid droplets to lysosomes for lipase-mediated hydrolysis, lipophagy mobilizes stored energy during fasting. The conservation from worms to mammals indicates an ancient and essential role for autophagy in lipid homeostasis. Defective lipophagy contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic disease in higher organisms.

label: DAF-2
description: DAF-2, the C. elegans insulin/IGF-1 receptor ortholog, partially regulates MXL-3 expression such that impaired insulin signaling leads to modest repression of mxl-3 transcription. This places MXL-3 downstream of the insulin-signaling axis that broadly controls metabolism and longevity in worms. The partial effect indicates that additional nutrient and developmental inputs also govern mxl-3, consistent with its role as a multifactorial repressor. The linkage reinforces the canonical insulin→autophagy/lipid regulatory cascade.

label: MXL-3 expression
description: DAF-2, the C. elegans insulin/IGF-1 receptor ortholog, partially regulates MXL-3 expression such that impaired insulin signaling leads to modest repression of mxl-3 transcription. This places MXL-3 downstream of the insulin-signaling axis that broadly controls metabolism and longevity in worms. The partial effect indicates that additional nutrient and developmental inputs also govern mxl-3, consistent with its role as a multifactorial repressor. The linkage reinforces the canonical insulin→autophagy/lipid regulatory cascade.

label: CeTOR
description: CeTOR, the C. elegans ortholog of mTOR, controls HLH-30 at the transcriptional level; inactivation of CeTOR induces hlh-30 expression, increasing the abundance of the master degradative transcription factor. This upstream control parallels mammalian mTORC1's post-translational repression of TFEB, adding a transcriptional layer in worms. By inducing HLH-30, CeTOR inhibition engages the full lysosomal-autophagic and lipolytic program. The relationship confirms mTOR as an evolutionarily conserved suppressor of the TFEB/HLH-30 axis.

label: HLH-30 transcription
description: CeTOR, the C. elegans ortholog of mTOR, controls HLH-30 at the transcriptional level; inactivation of CeTOR induces hlh-30 expression, increasing the abundance of the master degradative transcription factor. This upstream control parallels mammalian mTORC1's post-translational repression of TFEB, adding a transcriptional layer in worms. By inducing HLH-30, CeTOR inhibition engages the full lysosomal-autophagic and lipolytic program. The relationship confirms mTOR as an evolutionarily conserved suppressor of the TFEB/HLH-30 axis.

label: Starvation survival
description: HLH-30 is required for survival during prolonged starvation; hlh-30 mutant animals die prematurely under nutrient-deprived conditions due to their inability to mount sufficient autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization. By activating the clearance and energy-mobilization programs, HLH-30 enables worms to withstand food absence. This essential role mirrors the dependence of mammalian cells on TFEB for stress resilience. The phenotype establishes HLH-30 as a critical effector of adaptive starvation responses.

label: Peroxisome Biogenesis Network
description: The peroxisome biogenesis network receives material from autophagy when damaged peroxisomes are engulfed and fragmented, generating precursors that can be reassembled into functional peroxisomes. This autophagic-lysosomal processing of peroxisomal components allows recycling of membrane and matrix constituents to support new organelle formation. The relationship couples selective peroxisome degradation (pexophagy) to organelle turnover and renewal. It highlights autophagy's role not only in disposal but also in enabling peroxisome homeostasis.

label: PERO1
